````text
### TARGET BLOCK — write the questions about THIS text

[EN] Document: S/2011/16
  Title: Letter dated 10 January 2011 from the Permanent Representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General
The specific capacities that should be given primacy will vary from country to country. Certain institutions, however, are crucial to consolidating peace regardless of the country context, and significant efforts should be invested in their development.
They include: (a) institutions carrying out political functions (such as implementing peace agreements, elections, taking and implementing decisions, and carrying out leadership functions); (b) security and rule-of-law institutions; (c) public finance institutions; and (d) institutions entrusted with economic recovery and service delivery.
Debates about post-conflict institution-building often assume that the aforementioned functions are carried out only by State institutions. However, in reality, some of those functions are carried out partly or completely by various nonState actors, such as civil society and international organizations.
In many cases, civil society also acts as an additional pillar in institution-building by helping newly formed institutions to define agendas and priorities that are of direct benefit to citizens.
Effective oversight and accountability mechanisms are central to the legitimacy and credibility of the institutions.

### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS — none. The target block cites no other document available in the corpus.

### DOCUMENT CONTEXT — surrounding text of the SAME document, supporting context only. It resolves what the target block leaves implicit; it is never a source of answers.

[EN] Document S/2011/16 — surrounding passages
Letter dated 10 January 2011 from the Permanent Representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General
I have the honour to inform you that during the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Security Council is scheduled to hold an open debate on the theme "Post-conflict peacebuilding: institution-building" on Friday, 21 January 2011.
Bosnia and Herzegovina has prepared the attached concept note to help guide the discussion on this subject (see annex).
Ambassador
Post-conflict peacebuilding: institution-building
Security Council open debate: Bosnia and Herzegovina concept paper
Armed conflict not only causes the loss of human life and physical damage; it also has serious effects on Government institutions.
It tears the social fabric, deepens ethnic divisions and conflict among communities, and results in deaths and displacement among the population, thus destroying the basis for the functioning of institutions.
Such a lack of capacity greatly hinders a society's ability to restore and maintain peace.
This may be one of the main reasons why the majority of post-conflict countries experience a return to conflict within 10 years in spite of all the efforts to promote peace.
Consequently, an increasing emphasis has been placed on the crucial role of institutional development in preventing the renewal of conflict.

Those concerned with peacebuilding have come to recognize the importance of coordinated rapid action to support post-conflict Governments in building core State capacities.
If properly executed, such action can help restore security, legitimacy, accountability and effectiveness, thus delivering peace dividends that will enhance trust in national leadership.
The traditional approach to post-conflict recovery has been to focus on providing humanitarian relief and rehabilitation assistance from the outset, leaving the complex process of institution-building for a later stage.
However, as the Secretary-General underlines in his 2009 report on peacebuilding in the immediate aftermath of conflict, it is usually too late to start developing institutional capacities when peacebuilding efforts are already at the exit strategy phase.
Although threats to peace are greatest in the immediate post-conflict period, that time also offers the greatest opportunity to strengthen the national capacities needed to see peacebuilding efforts through.
The building of accountable, legitimate and resilient institutions should therefore be a strategic objective from the early stages of the process.
The international community should offer its support to post-conflict countries to help them achieve functional and effective governance.

Building institutional capacity is a difficult undertaking in any country. It becomes even more challenging, however, when placed in a post-conflict setting.
The root causes of violence remain long after the conclusion of ceasefires and peace accords, creating highly volatile environments.
Many of the resources indispensable to creating or rebuilding institutions, including physical infrastructure, social capital, financing and human capital, are greatly depleted by the previous conflict.
However, an additional look should be given to local capacities, taking into account the specificity of each situation.
The process is complex, involving multiple stakeholders and capacity issues, and the need to strike the right balance between achieving short-term results (such as providing basic services) and long-term capacity development including institutional reform.
Post-conflict institution-building represents a very broad task, owing to the fact that institutional gaps exist in virtually all sectors of society. This in turn requires a complex, comprehensive approach to developing capacity. At the same time, in order to ensure the success of peacebuilding efforts, priority has to be given to the development of those institutions that will prevent a relapse into conflict and secure the survival and renewed credibility and legitimacy of the State.

[... the TARGET BLOCK appears here ...]

Considering the weakened and vulnerable state of post-conflict countries, it may be tempting to transfer much of the responsibility for peacebuilding and consequently institution-building to the international community.
It is indeed appropriate in certain cases for the international community to set up transitional institutions and provide services that would be otherwise rendered through national capacities. However, the purpose of institution-building is to progressively reduce dependence on the international community and promote self-reliance.
National ownership is a sine qua non for the establishment of effective institutions and securing sustainable peace.
First and foremost, there must be at least a basic level of consensus and political will among the leading national stakeholders in order for institutional development to succeed.
Second, national actors have a far better knowledge of local conditions, which makes them more suitable to assess which institutional solutions will work in their particular context.
They are also aware of existing institutional resources, and their inclusion in the institution-building process can ensure that such resources are utilized to the greatest extent while preventing the creation of redundant capacity.
National ownership also facilitates the inclusion of all key stakeholder groups (such as all parties in the conflict, refugees and internally displaced persons, minorities and women) in designing and participating in future institutions.

The United Nations, Member States, regional organizations and international financial institutions also play a vital role in post-conflict institution-building.
Their objective in this process should be to facilitate and support programmes that lead to the creation of a stable, viable, and responsive state by working with domestic decision-making institutions.
Given the conditions in post-conflict environments, the best way to achieve that objective is by providing reliable, early and flexible funding, as well as a pool of civilian experts, particularly in the areas of justice, security sector reform, governance and economic recovery.
It is also important that the efforts of those various external actors are coordinated, primarily through the mechanisms of the United Nations, to avoid differing or overlapping courses of action.
International organizations should also bear in mind that they can make a significant contribution to institution-building and the peacebuilding process as a whole by making sure that domestic professionals have the incentives to remain within domestic structures, thus preventing "brain-drain".
Finally, the success of post-conflict institution-building depends on forging a partnership based on shared goals between the international community and a post-conflict society.

When domestic and international stakeholders build consensus on a set of goals, achieving those goals becomes a driving force for institution-building, thus stabilizing a post-conflict society by bringing all stakeholders together to collaborate on a shared agenda until the risk of future conflict is eliminated.
With regard to areas such as predictability of response and national capacity development, we support his recommendation that greater efforts are required from the United Nations, international financial institutions, Member States, regional organizations and civil society in order to reach an agreement on how we can work together to address the continuing challenges of post-conflict peacebuilding, including institution-building.
We hope for and encourage a fruitful exchange of views and valuable contributions from the Security Council during this debate.
The Security Council has already addressed a number of issues related to the theme of post-conflict institution-building. In this particular debate, it is expected to focus on the following questions as challenges in the further elaboration of the theme of post-conflict peacebuilding:

1. How effectively does the Security Council consider and reflect on the process of institution-building when preparing for all stages of a mission that are crucial for consolidating peace, taking into account the specificities of each country and situation?
2. Bearing in mind the importance of introducing national ownership when preparing and implementing institution-building tasks, is there a need to further consider how the United Nations and international community can assist in building upon existing national capacities and resources in a more efficient and coordinated manner?
3. How can the partnership between international actors be better defined in order to improve effective institution-building during the different phases of the process? What could be the role of the Security Council in enhancing this partnership?
4. What additional steps could be taken within the United Nations system for better, integrated and more coordinated approach for carrying out institution-building processes?
5. How can the advisory role of the Peacebuilding Commission, especially in terms of lessons learned, be more effectively used to enable the United Nations system to establish an integrated approach for institution-building and to address the gaps in transition?

HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document is, WHEN it is from — often the source of your time pin — and whether it belongs to a recurring series.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which parties "the sides" are, which regime a measure belongs to, who wrote the letter or report, the calendar dates that pin the question. If any part of the answer's substance sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument — an article of the Institution-Building Package, a paragraph of an earlier resolution, a rule from a statute — a norm-state question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument, whose own text is the better match in this corpus, so the gold would be wrong; ask instead about what THIS document does with it: what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.
THE DEFINING RULES — NO INSTRUMENT, NORM-STATE STANCE, TIME-PINNED:
1. NO INSTRUMENT REFERENCE. The question contains no resolution or decision number, no document symbol, no paragraph number, and no instrument used as a locator, by identifier or by description: not "under resolution 918 (1994)", not "under the 1994 Security Council resolution on Rwanda", not "under the Secretary-General's May 1994 report, what ceiling applied". If the question cannot be asked without pointing at an instrument, it belongs to the lookup mode — discard it here. Three things are not instrument references: bodies named after resolutions ("the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1533 (2004)", "the 1267 Committee") — a name, not a citation; dated-act time pins (rule 3); and the office-or-State-plus-date attribution of a finding or figure (ATTRIBUTION), which is part of the fact. Identifiers may appear inside the ANSWER span.
2. NORM-STATE STANCE. Ask what applied, was required, was in force, was due — not what an organ said, decided, requested, called for or continued to do. The organ may appear as the actor of the norm; the speech act is never the thing asked about. Banned forms: "What did the Security Council decide / request / authorize / encourage / reaffirm ...", "What were States called upon to consider ...", "What did [body] continue to do ...", "What role did [body] play ...", "What did the resolution say ...". Write the stance naturally: it is a perspective, not a template. "What duration applied to the informal interactive hearings?" is a calque — a specialist writes "How long were the informal interactive hearings to run?"; "What legal status applied to X?" is a calque — a specialist writes "Was X lawful ...?" or "Was X contrary to international law ...?". Yes/no questions are welcome and common ("Did the arms embargo on Rwanda cover non-governmental forces in May 1994?", "Was UNMIL's mandate still in force in June 2011?"); their answer is still the span of the block that decides the question, never "yes" or "no".
3. TIME PIN — MANDATORY. Every question carries an explicit absolute time anchor: a date ("as at 30 April 2011"), a month or year ("from May 1994", "in force in 2004"), or a dated act ("under the extension agreed in December 2011", "the measures imposed in May 1994", "extended on 30 June 2006"), taken from the block, the context or the metadata date. Document-relative time is forbidden — "current", "now", "recently", "the day before", "at its next session", "the reporting period", a date without a year: resolve or discard.
ANCHORS: besides the time pin, every question carries at least TWO substantive anchors in its own text, from: the regime or situation ("the arms embargo on Rwanda", "the Iran sanctions regime", "the Biological Weapons Convention"), the country or territory, the mission or body ("UNAMIR", "the Panel of Experts on the Sudan"), the actor bound or protected, or the measure or term of art at issue. The regime must be NAMED: "the Programme of Action" without "small arms and light weapons" fits the Barbados, Istanbul, Almaty and Durban Programmes of Action equally; "victims and witnesses" without "crimes by United Nations officials and experts on mission" is anchorless. Generic actors are not anchors: "States", "Member States", "the Secretary-General", "the Office of the High Commissioner". Every definite description is named in the question itself — never bare "the Committee", "the sides", "the Mission", "the Government". Report the anchors in "anchors" as verbatim substrings of the question; a phrase that appears only in the answer is not an anchor.
THE SIBLING TEST AND RECURRING SERIES — why the pin and the anchors exist: UN norms recur by design. The same mandate is renewed year after year in near-identical words, so "What troop ceiling applied to UNMISS?" has a different answer for every renewal — the time pin picks the year. The same asset-freeze, travel-ban and reporting clauses are cloned across regimes, so "Who was exempt from the travel ban?" fits a dozen regimes — the regime anchor picks the one. Know the recurring families: session-numbered General Assembly resolutions on standing agenda items (human rights in a country, the right to food, the right to development, assistance to Non-Self-Governing Territories, the Biological and Chemical Weapons Conventions, New Caledonia, criminal accountability of UN officials, the rule of law); the annual ECOSOC and Assembly resolutions on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and the occupied Syrian Golan; the biennial "cooperation between the United Nations and [regional organization]" resolutions; the biennial programme-planning and pattern-of-conferences resolutions; mandate renewals; International Day resolutions; monthly and periodic reports. For these, the year alone is not enough when the paragraph is unchanged year to year: ask only about content specific to THIS instance — a date, a figure, a newly added task, a named event. A monthly KFOR report recurs, but its troop figure is this month's own. Before keeping a question ask: would it, word for word, be an equally sensible question about last year's renewal or another regime's twin? If yes, add what is missing, target this instance's content, or skip with skip_reason "recurring boilerplate". Apply the same test to the answer in its question context: recurring wording alone does not distinguish an instance; a short answer remains valid when the question pins down a specific measure, event or figure.
CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT ONLY:
- QUALIFYING spans: measures imposed, extended or terminated; mandate scope and tasks; conditions, criteria, exemptions; deadlines and mandate periods; ceilings, appropriations, contributions, reported figures; appointments, composition, procedures; concrete dated events and determinations.
- DISQUALIFIED spans, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; reaffirms a determination first made elsewhere; reaffirms a request to CONTINUE an activity; encourages or invites in general terms; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; recommends that Governments accord priority; commemorations and anniversaries; aspirations; preambular recitals.
ATTRIBUTION: reports state the reporting body's findings and letters convey positions; a finding or figure stays attributed and dated, to the OFFICE or STATE, never a bare personal name — "According to KFOR's report for February 2007, were any incidents against KFOR recorded in Kosovo?" An agentless passive is stripped attribution: "was proposed", "were recorded", "was reported" without the proposer, recorder or reporter — name the source from the block. The finding must be a figure, event or determination a practitioner would verify, never rhetoric; never present an attributed claim as established fact.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST — the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. Four ways to fail it:
- Restatement: the answer repeats the question's words or the pointer it was built from ("the exemptions established by the Committee" for "what exemptions applied").
- Guessability: a specialist could complete the answer from the question with better than even odds ("one-day" for the duration of informal hearings; "in writing" for the form of a request).
- Answer scaffolding: the question was formed by truncating the answer span and interrogating its tail. Rebuild from the need, not from the span's syntax.
- Deictic answer: the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document — "the above priorities", "as adopted in the present resolution", "the measures set out below". Discard, or narrow to a self-contained span.
CORE RULES:
- Smallest Unit: exactly ONE norm element or fact per question — one deadline, one figure, one criterion, one exemption, one actor, one condition. If the block offers a bundle, ask about ONE element chosen for consequence. Prefer questions whose complete answer is a short span; if the natural answer is a paragraph or a long list, narrow or discard.
- Wording & Length: direct interrogative, 8–20 words, hard maximum 25.
- Diversity: the questions must target different facts; if two or more pairs pass every rule, span at least two categories.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — eight categories ("question_type"), in priority order, each with the norm-state shapes practitioners use for it:
  1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures in force, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "What exemptions applied to [measure] in [year]?", "Under what conditions was [measure] to be reviewed as of [date]?", "Did the arms embargo on [country] cover [actors] in [month year]?"
  2. date_deadline_or_mandate — mandate start, extension and expiry; reporting and compliance deadlines; effective and review dates: "By what date was [actor] required to [X], as of [year]?", "Until when was [mission]'s mandate extended on [date]?", "Was [mission]'s mandate still in force in [month year]?"
  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations, assessed and outstanding contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What troop ceiling applied to [mission] from [month year]?", "What amount of [contributions] was outstanding as at [date]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — reporting duties and frequency, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] required to report on [X] in [year]?", "Who was to verify [X] under [dated act]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, formally defined terms: "Who was responsible for [X] in [year]?", "Which body decided [X] as of [date]?"
  6. situation_scope_or_coverage — what a measure covered: country, territory, population, period, carve-outs: "What did [mission]'s mandate cover from [date]?", "Did [measure] apply to [territory] in [year]?"
  7. operative_action, recast as norm-state — the obligation, task or authorization in force, not the act of deciding it: "What was [party] required to do by [date] under [dated act]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated figures, incidents and determinations, attributed to office or State: "According to [office]'s [month year] report, what was [figure] as at [date]?", "According to [State]'s [month year] letter, did [X] happen?"
Purpose or rationale only when the block states it explicitly and completely.

REAL FAILURES FROM PREVIOUS RUNS — never reproduce these patterns:
✗ "In 2004, what issue were Governments to prioritize in specialized agencies for Non-Self-Governing Territories?" — answer "the question of providing assistance to the peoples of the Non-Self-Governing Territories" → the span is "Recommends that all Governments ... accord priority" (DISQUALIFIED), the resolution recurs annually with this paragraph unchanged, and the answer restates the question. ✗ "In 2012, what legal status applied to Israel's wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem?" — answer "is contrary to international law" → "Also reaffirms that ..." is an annual reaffirmation of a determination first made elsewhere, and "what legal status applied" is a calque. Skip; the norm's home is the ICJ advisory opinion, not this year's restatement.
✗ "In 2013, what duration applied to informal interactive hearings for the high-level dialogue on international migration and development?" — answer "one-day" → a calque, and a coin-flip answer. Even as "How long were the informal interactive hearings for the 2013 high-level dialogue on international migration and development to run?", INFORMATIVENESS counsels skipping.
✗ "What did the Forum Ministerial Committee continue to do in New Caledonia in 2010?" → "What did X continue to do" is a comprehension frame, the span is "welcomes the continuing role" (ceremony), and the paragraph recurs in every annual New Caledonia resolution. Skip.
✗ "In 2011, what jurisdiction were States called upon to consider accepting?" → speech-act stance; "calls upon States to consider" is a soft invitation, not a norm; the anchor listed ("International Court of Justice") appears only in the answer. Discard.
✗ "By what deadline were States parties to submit annual information and data to the Implementation Support Unit?" → no regime named (the CCW has an Implementation Support Unit too), no year, and the clause recurs annually. Fix: "As of 2012, what annual deadline applied to confidence-building measure returns from States parties to the Biological Weapons Convention?"
✗ "What protection were States to provide to victims and witnesses in 2013?" → the anchors reported ("crimes of a serious nature", "United Nations officials and experts on mission") are not in the question, which is therefore anchorless; the paragraph recurs annually. Fix: "In 2013, what protection were States to provide to witnesses to crimes by United Nations officials and experts on mission?" — then skip unless that paragraph changed this year.
✗ "What military measure was proposed against Eritrea in December 2009?" → "was proposed" hides the proposer, the fact a sanctions lawyer needs. Name the proposer from the block; likewise "Were any incidents against KFOR recorded in Kosovo in February 2007?" hides the recorder until it reads "According to KFOR's report for February 2007, ...".
✗ "What troop ceiling did resolution 918 (1994) authorize for UNAMIR?" and "What troop ceiling did the 1994 Security Council resolution on Rwanda authorize?" → instrument citation and instrument description: lookup mode. "What is UNAMIR's authorized troop ceiling?" → no time pin; the norm is re-stated in every renewal. Fix: "What troop ceiling applied to UNAMIR from May 1994?"
✗ "What was the current ceiling for the least developed countries' rate of assessment?" → "current" is document-relative. Fix: "What ceiling applied to the least developed countries' rate of assessment in 2005?"
SELF-CHECK every question, in this order:
1. Unchanged recurring text? A quoted provision of another instrument as the target? → skip or reframe to what this document does with it.
2. No instrument reference — no number, symbol, paragraph number or instrument description as locator; only resolution-named bodies, dated-act pins and office-or-State-plus-date attributions.
3. Norm-state stance, written naturally — no "what did X decide / request / call upon / continue to do / say", no "what duration / status applied" calque; a yes/no question answered by a deciding span.
4. Absolute time pin present; no document-relative time anywhere.
5. Two substantive anchors in the question, regime named, reported verbatim; every definite description named; SIBLING TEST passed, with this instance's own content where the series recurs.
6. Answer span QUALIFYING, not a softer ceremonial form or an annual reaffirmation; finding attributed to office or State, no agentless passive; INFORMATIVENESS passed — no restatement, no guessable answer, no answer scaffolding, no deictic span.
7. BLOCK TEST: answer fully in the block, not from a reference, the context or metadata.
8. One smallest-unit fact; 8–20 words (max 25); terms of art verbatim, paraphrase without drift; figures exact in the answer. Fewer than three passed? Output fewer. None? Output the skip.

You are an expert at creating semantic retrieval questions for United Nations documents (resolutions, reports, letters, and meeting records).
THE INFORMATION NEED OF THIS MODE: every question is a query typed by a searcher who knows the SITUATION and what they need to find out, but not the corpus's vocabulary and not which instrument governs — a desk officer new to a file, a journalist, a researcher approaching a regime from outside its terminology. Their query carries meaning, not the documents' exact words; the retrieval system must match concept to text. Write from that need: a real question about a situation, the response to it, or the people affected — never a report of what a body or a speaker SAID, never a reading-comprehension question about what the passage says. The mode stays conceptual, but it still needs a concrete anchor and a year, because a query that matches everything finds nothing.
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English. In the ANSWER, reproduce dates, durations, amounts, percentages and thresholds exactly. Use the official English names of organs, bodies, missions and instruments, never literal translations.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document is, when it is from and whether it belongs to a recurring series; the subject-matter words of its title ("the situation in Rwanda") may serve as topic words in a question.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which committee "the Committee" is, which State "the speaker" represents, who wrote the letter, the calendar year of the meeting, report or session. If any needed fact, figure, list or reason sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument, a question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument; ask instead about what THIS document does with it — what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.
DEFINING RULES OF THIS MODE:
1. NO IDENTIFIERS: no resolution or decision number, document symbol or paragraph number in a question, and no deixis — "this resolution", "the present report", "this document", the document's contents as if visible. Identifiers may appear inside the answer span.
2. CONCEPTUAL, NOT EXTRACTIVE: the question targets a situation, a mechanism or an affected party; it never asks for a datum by its name — "what troop ceiling", "by what date", "what amount", "which official" belong to another mode. The span that answers a conceptual question may still contain a figure ("an estimated 250,000 refugees"). If the block offers only data points, skip with skip_reason "extractive only".
3. THE YEAR IS MANDATORY: every question carries an absolute year, date or dated period ("in 2009", "in spring 1994", "after the 2011 legislative elections"), taken from the block, the context or the metadata. Without it, a question about a mission, a regime or a recurring resolution has one answer per year and therefore none.
4. NOT A SPEECH REPORT: never "How did [State/body] describe ...", "What did [body] say about ...", "What caution / warning did [body] give ...", "What did [body] stress ...", "What did the speaker say ...". Ask about the situation, the response or the affected party itself; what attributed content may be asked about, and how, is set out under ATTRIBUTION.
LEXICAL DISTANCE — the retriever must match on meaning, not keyword overlap. Distance comes from describing the SITUATION, RESPONSE or PEOPLE in ordinary words instead of the document's formulas — "the mass killing of civilians" for "the very numerous killings of civilians"; "UN peacekeepers" for the mission's formal designation; "people who fled across the border" for "refugees who crossed the border" — and never from lifting the block's phrasing or reproducing a list it gives. Distance must NOT come from renaming terms of art or official names: "arms embargo" is not "weapons ban", "asset freeze" is not "account blocking"; an International Day, a body, a mission keeps its name (an official acronym may be expanded). A substituted term changes what is being asked about; legal and diplomatic text is sensitive to exact words — when unsure whether a word is load-bearing, keep it. Paraphrase never strips the discriminating anchor: keep the country, the mission and the year.
ANCHOR — the person typing has not seen this document and is searching among hundreds of thousands of UN documents in the same formulaic register. Every question carries at least one concrete anchor: a country or situation ("Rwanda", "the conflict in Darfur"), a mission or operation ("UNAMIR"), a named body or actor type ("the Panel of Experts on the Sudan", "troop-contributing countries"), or a subject matter tied to a situation ("arms embargo exemptions for humanitarian equipment in Somalia"). A bare topic ("counterterrorism measures", "climate action", "developing countries", "human rights learning") is not an anchor. Every definite description is named in the question itself — never bare "the Committee", "the Regional Centre", "the speaker", "the sides", "the Council". Report the anchor in "anchor" as a verbatim substring of the question. The test: typed into a search engine by a stranger, would the question lead to THIS document's subject matter? "What did the Security Council express grave concern about?" fails; "How did the Security Council respond to attacks on displaced civilians in Rwanda in May 1994?" passes.
RECURRING SERIES — know the families: session-numbered General Assembly resolutions on standing agenda items (a country's human rights situation, the right to food, the right to development, human rights learning, the Chemical and Biological Weapons Conventions, New Caledonia); the annual ECOSOC and Assembly resolutions on the Occupied Palestinian Territory; the biennial "cooperation between the United Nations and [regional organization]" resolutions, whose consultation clauses are cloned across the OSCE, CIS, SCO, EurAsEC and every other partner; mandate renewals; International Day resolutions; periodic reports. An unchanged paragraph in such a series fits every year — and every partner organization — equally, even with the year attached; the same holds for any span that could appear unchanged in dozens of UN documents (stakeholder invitation lists, cooperate-and-collaborate lists, the universal "measures must comply with international law" clause, "primary responsibility lies with the authorities themselves"). Ask only about content specific to THIS instance — a named event, a new task, a figure; if the block holds only unchanged recurring text, skip with skip_reason "recurring boilerplate". When a block holds both ceremony and substance, ask about the substance.
CONSEQUENTIAL ANSWER SPANS:
- QUALIFYING: measures established, extended or modified; mandates and their scope; conditions, criteria and exemptions; how a mechanism operates; who is bound, protected or assisted and how; concrete reported events, findings and stated rationales; and, for situation-framed questions, preambular ASSESSMENTS that state concretely what is happening ("delays by the signatory parties and the absence of an inclusive political settlement", "an estimated 250,000 refugees crossed the border").
- DISQUALIFIED, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; encourages or invites in general terms; invites two officials to hold regular consultations; calls upon bodies to support, cooperate and collaborate with stakeholders; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; aspirations. Preambular RECITALS — recalling, reaffirming, recognizing responsibility, expressing concern — are framing, not answer material, even though preambular ASSESSMENTS are.
ATTRIBUTION — much of this corpus reports what someone SAID. When the block attributes a statement, claim, estimate or assessment, the question and answer preserve the attribution — to the STATE, the OFFICE ("the representative of South Africa", "the Secretary-General"), or, for a Secretariat report, "UN reporting" — never a bare personal name. An agentless passive or a claim stated as fact is stripped attribution: "as weapons kept reaching the separatists" presents Georgia's assertion as fact — write "according to Georgia" or "in Georgia's account". Attributed content is askable only as a State's position on an identifiable proposal, instrument or measure ("What position did Guyana take on the use of force in Kosovo in 1999?"), a stated rationale, or a concrete situation assessment — never a characterization ("how did Guyana describe the crisis"), an aspiration, a courtesy or a generic exhortation. OWN ACTS NEED NO HEDGE: a concrete, completed act of the author's own side — France's letter recounting that the European Union adopted a disarmament plan endorsed by its Heads of State — may be asked about directly; the requirement targets contested claims and characterizations of others.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST: the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. It fails when the answer restates the question's words or the pointer it was built from, when a reader could guess it from the question with better than even odds, or when the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document ("the above priorities", "as adopted in the present resolution"). Discard, or ask about the substance instead.
CORE RULES:
- Single Intent, Short Span: one clear informational goal per question — broader than a single fact is fine, bundled asks are not — answered by a short contiguous span of the block; if the only span is a whole paragraph, narrow the question or discard.
- Wording & Length: natural search phrasing, 8–20 words, hard maximum 25.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — three framings ("framing"); the questions must target distinguishable aspects and, when generating more than one pair, span at least two of them:
  1. situation — context or problem: what crisis, threat, dispute or development does the document respond to or describe? The motivating concern behind a measure, and the state of affairs a report or preamble concretely assesses.
  2. response — mechanism or action: what mission, measure, process or institutional arrangement is established, extended or modified, and how does it operate?
  3. stakeholder — affected party or scenario: who is bound, sanctioned, protected or assisted, and in what real-world scenario? The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which parties "the sides" are, which committee "the Committee" is, what a cited instrument is, the organ, type, date and identifier of this document. If any part of the answer's substance sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers, even when the cited text is supplied: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument — an article of the Institution-Building Package, a paragraph of an earlier resolution, a rule from a statute — a question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument; ask instead about what THIS document does with it: alleges, applies, reports, contests, amends. Never ask about the metadata itself.
THE DEFINING RULE — TWO RENDERINGS OF EACH QUESTION:
- "question": names the instrument BY DESCRIPTION — organ + year + subject ("the 2004 Security Council resolution on Lebanese sovereignty", "the Secretary-General's July 1999 report on Iraq's oil industry", "the 17 June 2014 New Agenda Coalition working paper on transparency in nuclear disarmament"). No identifier of any kind in this rendering. When same-year instruments share a situation, the subject words must pick THIS one out — "the 2011 Security Council resolution establishing the no-fly zone over Libya", not "the 2011 Security Council resolution on Libya".
- DESCRIPTION ACCURACY: describe the instrument AS IT IS, from the metadata — adopting organ and document type, never omitted ("the 2008 resolution on ..." is incomplete: whose?). A letter is described by date, sender and subject ("the 28 July 2014 letter from Israel on the special session"), with the addressee added when the sender wrote more than one letter on the subject — never "the Security Council letter". A resolution that defers a draft and annexes it is "the 2006 General Assembly resolution deferring consideration of the draft declaration on indigenous peoples", never "the 2006 General Assembly declaration": an annexed draft is not an adopted instrument.
- "question_cited": the same words with the description swapped for the exact official identifier, in natural practitioner phrasing ("in resolution 918 (1994)", "in S/1999/746", "in CD/1989"). The slot is the whole instrument phrase; in the cited rendering it is the identifier, optionally preceded by the source-type words ("the Secretary-General's report S/1999/746" — required for attributed figures, so the office survives). Copy the identifier exactly from the block, a resolved reference or the metadata. Identifier scope: resolution and decision numbers, and report, letter, working-paper and meeting-record symbols, including PV/SR symbols.
- THE SLOT IS A LOCATOR, NOT A SPEAKER: the instrument tells the searcher where the fact lives. The organ acts ("what did the Security Council authorize for UNAMIR in [instrument]?"); for an operative act, "did [instrument] extend / impose / authorize ..." is accepted practitioner shorthand; the instrument never speaks — no "what did [the resolution / it] say, state, mention, note", and no bare "it" for the instrument.
- Everything else is named OUTSIDE the slot so it survives the swap: "the Security Council", never "the Council"; the actor; the anchor. The description's year is the base rendering's time pin; if the identifier carries no year and the question holds no other absolute date, add one, in both renderings.
- Why two renderings: an identifier is a language-invariant string, identical in every language version, so the cited rendering can be matched by string overlap alone; the description must be matched semantically, across languages. The pair isolates exactly what the string buys.
ANCHOR, SIBLING TEST, RECURRING SERIES:

A generic actor is never the anchor: not "the Secretary-General", "Member States", "States parties", "the Council", "the Office of the High Commissioner". Report it in "anchor" exactly as it appears in the base rendering.
- SIBLING TEST: UN documents repeat by design — the same mandate renewed every year in near-identical words, the same asset-freeze and travel-ban clauses cloned across sanctions regimes, one skeleton for every International Day resolution. Set the instrument wording aside, retain its resolved absolute time pin, and ask: would the rest of the question be an equally sensible question about a different renewal or a different situation's twin? If yes, add what is missing or discard. Repeated generic wording in the answer span cannot by itself justify a question, even in an operative paragraph. A short figure, date, condition or named actor may still qualify when the question uniquely anchors the specific measure, event or reporting instance; unchanged recurring boilerplate remains disqualified.
- RECURRING SERIES — know the families: session-numbered General Assembly resolutions on a standing agenda item (human rights in a country, the right to food, the right to development, assistance to Non-Self-Governing Territories, the Chemical and Biological Weapons Conventions, New Caledonia, criminal accountability of UN officials); the annual ECOSOC and Assembly resolutions on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and the occupied Syrian Golan; the biennial "cooperation between the United Nations and [regional organization]" resolutions; the biennial programme-planning and pattern-of-conferences resolutions; mandate renewals; International Day resolutions; monthly and periodic reports. The title and context reveal the family. For such blocks, ask only about content specific to THIS instance — a date, a figure, a newly added task, a named event: a monthly KFOR report recurs, but its troop figure is this month's own. A paragraph unchanged from instance to instance fails the sibling test even with the year attached; if the block holds only such text, return [{"skip_reason": "recurring boilerplate"}].
TIME: every temporal expression in the QUESTION is absolute. Never "current", "now", "recently", "today", "the day before", "at its next session", "last month", "the reporting period", or a date without a year; resolve them into calendar terms from the block, context and metadata, or discard.
CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT ONLY — a question is worth asking only when its answer span carries operational or legal effect or a concrete fact:
- QUALIFYING spans: decides, authorizes, establishes, extends, terminates, imposes, proclaims, designates, appoints, appropriates, approves; requests or directs WITH a named deliverable or deadline; specific demands addressed to a named party; conditions, criteria and exemptions; exact figures, dates, ceilings, appropriations; named actors and formally defined terms; concrete reported events and findings.
- DISQUALIFIED spans, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; reaffirms a request to CONTINUE an activity; encourages or invites in general terms; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; recommends that Governments accord priority; commemorations and anniversaries; aspirations and hopes; preambular recitals.
ATTRIBUTION: letters convey positions and reports state the reporting body's findings. When the block attributes a claim, estimate or assessment, the question and answer preserve the attribution — to the STATE or OFFICE ("the Secretary-General", "the United States delegation", "KFOR"), never a bare personal name (a name may appear only beside the office). An agentless passive is stripped attribution: "was proposed", "were recorded", "was reported" without the proposer, recorder or reporter — name the source. Attributed content is askable only as a position on an identifiable proposal, instrument or measure, a stated rationale, or a concrete figure or event; never present it as established fact.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST — the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. Four ways to fail it:
- Restatement: the answer repeats the question's words or the pointer it was built from — "a standard reporting form" in reply to "what reporting form were the nuclear-weapon States encouraged to agree on".
- Guessability: a specialist could complete the answer from the question with better than even odds — "the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development" when the question already says 2011 and the right to development.
- Answer scaffolding: the question was formed by truncating the answer span and interrogating its tail — "Which competence did France recognize for treaty bodies?" carved from "recognizes the competence of the treaty bodies to receive individual complaints". Rebuild from the need, not from the span's syntax.
- Deictic answer: the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document — "the above priorities", "the strategic framework as adopted in the present resolution", "the measures set out below". Discard, or narrow to a self-contained span.
CORE RULES:
- Single Focus, Smallest Unit: exactly ONE piece of information per question — one deadline, one figure, one criterion, one exemption, one actor. Prefer questions whose complete answer is a short span; if the natural answer is a paragraph or a long list, narrow or discard.
- Wording & Length: direct interrogative, 8–20 words per rendering, hard maximum 25.
- Diversity: the questions must target different facts and, when generating more than one pair, span at least two categories.

  1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures imposed, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "Which measures did the Security Council impose on [regime] in [instrument]?", "Under what condition was [X] to be [Y] under [instrument]?", "Did [instrument] extend the arms embargo on [regime] to [actors]?"
  2. date_deadline_or_mandate — mandate start, extension, expiry; reporting and compliance deadlines; effective and review dates: "By what date was [actor] to [X] under [instrument]?", "Until when did [instrument] extend [mission]'s mandate?"
  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations and contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What force level did the Security Council authorize for [mission] in [instrument]?", "What amount was appropriated for [X] in [instrument]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — who reports to whom and how often, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] to report to the Security Council on [X] under [instrument]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — named officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, defined terms: "Which body was tasked with [X] in [instrument]?" — never the identity of a briefer or speaker, which no practitioner needs.
  6. operative_action — what the organ decides, authorizes, demands or requests, and of whom, when it qualifies under CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT: "What did the Security Council demand of [party] in [instrument]?"
  7. situation_scope_or_coverage — which country, territory, population or period a measure or report covers; carve-outs: "Did [instrument] cover [territory / population]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated facts and conclusions, attributed, only facts a practitioner would verify: "According to [described report], what was [figure] as at [date]?" — cited form "According to the Secretary-General's report S/1999/746, ...".
Yes/no questions are welcome and common; their answer is still the span of the block that decides the question, never "yes" or "no". A bare slot ("What was to be considered ...?", "What did the Assembly request ...?" with no named subject) is not a question.

THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument, a question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument; ask instead about what THIS document does with it — what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.

WHAT TO ASK — eight categories ("question_type"), in priority order, each with the shapes practitioners use for it:
  1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures imposed, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "Which measures did the Security Council impose on [regime] in [instrument]?", "Under what condition was [X] to be [Y] under [instrument]?", "Did [instrument] extend the arms embargo on [regime] to [actors]?"
  2. date_deadline_or_mandate — mandate start, extension, expiry; reporting and compliance deadlines; effective and review dates: "By what date was [actor] to [X] under [instrument]?", "Until when did [instrument] extend [mission]'s mandate?"
  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations and contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What force level did the Security Council authorize for [mission] in [instrument]?", "What amount was appropriated for [X] in [instrument]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — who reports to whom and how often, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] to report to the Security Council on [X] under [instrument]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — named officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, defined terms: "Which body was tasked with [X] in [instrument]?" — never the identity of a briefer or speaker, which no practitioner needs.
  6. operative_action — what the organ decides, authorizes, demands or requests, and of whom, when it qualifies under CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT: "What did the Security Council demand of [party] in [instrument]?"
  7. situation_scope_or_coverage — which country, territory, population or period a measure or report covers; carve-outs: "Did [instrument] cover [territory / population]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated facts and conclusions, attributed, only facts a practitioner would verify: "According to [described report], what was [figure] as at [date]?" — cited form "According to the Secretary-General's report S/1999/746, ...".

Resolution 1353 (2001)
Adopted by the Security Council at its 4326th meeting, on 13 June 2001
The Security Council,
Reaffirming its resolutions 1318 (2000) of 7 September 2000 and 1327 (2000) of 13 November 2000 and the statements by its President of 3 May 1994 (S/PRST/1994/22) and 28 March 1996 (S/PRST/1996/13), and all other relevant statements by its President,

Reaffirming its primary responsibility under the Charter of the United Nations for the maintenance of international peace and security, reiterating its commitment to enhance the capacity of the United Nations in this area, and emphasizing its willingness to take all necessary steps within its competence to that end,
Recalling the relevant recommendations in the report of the Panel on United Nations Peace Operations (S/2000/809), and reaffirming its support for all efforts to strengthen the efficiency and effectiveness of United Nations peacekeeping operations,
Stressing the need to ensure the safety and security of peacekeepers and other United Nations and associated personnel, including humanitarian personnel,
Stressing the need to improve the relationship between the Security Council, the troop-contributing countries and the Secretariat to foster a spirit of partnership, cooperation, confidence and mutual trust,
Recognizing the need to strengthen cooperation with troop-contributing countries, as part of a series of measures to ensure more coherent and integrated concepts of operations and to enhance managerial efficiency and operational effectiveness of United Nations peacekeeping operations,

Noting that relevant provisions contained in the annexes to the present resolution pertain also to strengthening cooperation with countries contributing civilian police and other personnel,
1. Agrees to adopt the decisions and recommendations contained in the annexes to the present resolution;
2. Requests its Working Group on Peacekeeping Operations to continue its work on strengthening the capacity of the United Nations to establish and support efficient and effective peacekeeping operations;
3. 4. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.
Annex I
The Security Council 1. Recognizes that its partnership with troop-contributing countries can be strengthened by the assumption by Member States, in particular those with the greatest capacity and means to do so, of their shared responsibility to provide personnel, assistance and facilities to the United Nations for the maintenance of international peace and security;

2. Encourages Member States to take steps to bridge the commitment gap with regard to personnel and equipment for specific United Nations peacekeeping operations;
3. Emphasizes the importance of troop-contributing countries taking the necessary and appropriate steps to ensure the capability of their peacekeepers to fulfil the missions' mandate, and underlines the importance of bilateral and international cooperation in this regard, including in the area of training, logistics and equipment;
4. Underlines the importance of ensuring that national contingents participating in United Nations peacekeeping operations receive effective and appropriate support from the Secretariat, including in the area of training, logistics and equipment;
5. Stresses the need to ensure that the Secretariat is given sufficient human and financial resources to fulfil these tasks, and that these resources be used efficiently and effectively;
6. Underlines that consultations between the Security Council, the Secretariat and troop-contributing countries should enhance the ability of the Security Council to make appropriate, effective and timely decisions in fulfilling its responsibilities;

7. Underlines also the need to maintain a comprehensive approach to improving the effectiveness of peacekeeping operations from their conception, including in preparing contingency plans for volatile situations, and promoting cohesive exit strategies; B
Operational issues
1. Encourages international cooperation and support for peacekeeping training, including the establishment of regional peacekeeping training centres, and stresses the need for technical support from the Secretary-General to such centres;
2. Requests the Secretary-General to include information on his consultations with troop-contributing countries in his regular reports to the Security Council on individual peacekeeping operations, and undertakes to take account of the views expressed in these consultations and in its meetings with troop-contributing countries when taking decisions on such operations;
3. Also requests the Secretary-General to convene assessments meetings with interested delegations, in particular troop-contributing countries, at appropriate stages of each peacekeeping operation as a part of his efforts to draw the lessons that can be learned, which should be taken into account in the conduct and planning of current and future operations;

4. Further requests the Secretary-General to take into account in the conduct of peacekeeping operations and in the regular lessons-learned process, the operational experiences of national contingents while in the field or following departure;
5. Undertakes to inform troop-contributing countries fully of the terms of reference of missions of the Security Council involving peacekeeping operations and subsequently of the conclusions of the missions;
6. Expresses its view that the conduct of reconnaissance visits to the mission area by countries committing troops can be highly valuable in preparing for effective participation in peacekeeping operations, and encourages support for such visits;
7. Urges the Secretary-General to take further steps to implement the proposal of the Panel on United Nations Peace Operations to create integrated mission task forces, and to pursue other related capabilities to improve United Nations planning and support capacities;
8. Stresses the need to improve the information and the analysis capacity of the United Nations Secretariat, with a view to improving the quality of advice to the Secretary-General, the Security Council and the troop-contributing countries;

9. Stresses also that the Secretariat's advice to the Security Council and the troop-contributing countries should include a range of recommendations for action on the basis of an objective assessment of the situation on the ground, rather than what Member States are presumed to be willing to support;
10. Underlines the importance of an effective mission-specific public information and communications capacity within peacekeeping operations, in particular through campaigns to improve awareness of the objectives and scope of the mission within the local population in the mission area;
11. Stresses the need for an effective public information programme to generate international public support for United Nations peacekeeping operations, and stresses also in this regard the need for special programmes, in particular in troop-contributing countries, to project the contribution of peacekeepers;
12. Underlines in this regard the need for an effective public information capacity within the United Nations, and takes note in this regard of the proposals made by the Secretary-General to strengthen Secretariat planning and support for public information in peacekeeping operations (S/2000/1081); C

Other mechanisms
1. Undertakes to continue to consider the possibility of using the Military Staff Committee as one of the means of enhancing United Nations peacekeeping operations;
2. Decides to strengthen cooperation with the troop-contributing countries in addition to and on the basis of the principles and provisions contained in the resolution and the present annex by improving and expanding existing consultation mechanisms as elaborated in annex II, with a view to ensuring proper reflection of the views and concerns of troop-contributing countries.

Format, procedures and documentation of meetings with the troop-contributing countries
The consultations with troop-contributing countries will take place in the following formats:

B. Consultation meetings with the troop-contributing countries;

Meetings between the Secretariat and troop-contributing countries
The Security Council supports the existing practice of meetings between the Secretariat and troop-contributing countries to discuss matters concerning specific peacekeeping operations, and also the participation at such meetings, where appropriate, of Special Representatives of the Secretary-General, Force Commanders and Civilian Police Commissioners.
Other forms of consultations
The Security Council notes that the forms of consultations mentioned herein are not exhaustive and that consultations may take a variety of other forms, including formal or informal communication between the President of the Council or its members, the Secretary-General and the troop-contributing countries and, as appropriate, with other countries especially affected, including countries from the region concerned.

You are an expert at creating legal retrieval questions from United Nations documents (resolutions, reports, letters, and meeting records).
PRACTITIONER MODE — THE SPECIALIST ASKS FOR THE STATE OF THE LAW, NOT FOR A DOCUMENT: every question is a query from a specialist who works the regime — sanctions counsel, a desk lawyer, a compliance officer, a peacekeeping legal adviser. No instrument is in their head; the NORM is. They ask what applied, who was bound, by when something was due, under what conditions something changed, what a mandate covered, what a figure stood at — at a point in time. The document is merely where the answer lives; the question never uses a document as a locator. A dated report or letter may appear solely to attribute a finding (ATTRIBUTION). The test throughout: would a regime specialist plausibly type roughly these words while advising on compliance, reviewing a mandate, or reconstructing what applied at a given date?
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English. In the ANSWER, reproduce dates, durations, amounts, percentages, troop figures and thresholds exactly. Use the official English names of organs, bodies, missions and instruments, never literal translations.
PARAPHRASE WITHOUT DRIFT: paraphrase the ordinary scaffolding around the norm; never lift multi-word descriptive fragments from the block as question scaffolding, and never reproduce a list the block gives. Copy terms of art and proper nouns exactly ("asset freeze", "safe humanitarian areas", "assessed contributions", "compensated without further action"). A paraphrase must not widen, narrow or shift the norm: "when the Secretary-General compensated an applicant" is not "when the Secretary-General decided the applicant be compensated without further action" — the first describes any payment, the second the specific statutory option the cap attaches to. Legal text is sensitive to exact words — when unsure whether a word is load-bearing, keep it.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document is, WHEN it is from — often the source of your time pin — and whether it belongs to a recurring series.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which parties "the sides" are, which regime a measure belongs to, who wrote the letter or report, the calendar dates that pin the question. If any part of the answer's substance sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument — an article of the Institution-Building Package, a paragraph of an earlier resolution, a rule from a statute — a norm-state question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument, whose own text is the better match in this corpus, so the gold would be wrong; ask instead about what THIS document does with it: what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.
THE DEFINING RULES — NO INSTRUMENT, NORM-STATE STANCE, TIME-PINNED:
1. NO INSTRUMENT REFERENCE. The question contains no resolution or decision number, no document symbol, no paragraph number, and no instrument used as a locator, by identifier or by description: not "under resolution 918 (1994)", not "under the 1994 Security Council resolution on Rwanda", not "under the Secretary-General's May 1994 report, what ceiling applied". If the question cannot be asked without pointing at an instrument, it belongs to the lookup mode — discard it here. Three things are not instrument references: bodies named after resolutions ("the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1533 (2004)", "the 1267 Committee") — a name, not a citation; dated-act time pins (rule 3); and the office-or-State-plus-date attribution of a finding or figure (ATTRIBUTION), which is part of the fact. Identifiers may appear inside the ANSWER span.
2. NORM-STATE STANCE. Ask what applied, was required, was in force, was due — not what an organ said, decided, requested, called for or continued to do. The organ may appear as the actor of the norm; the speech act is never the thing asked about. Banned forms: "What did the Security Council decide / request / authorize / encourage / reaffirm ...", "What were States called upon to consider ...", "What did [body] continue to do ...", "What role did [body] play ...", "What did the resolution say ...". Write the stance naturally: it is a perspective, not a template. "What duration applied to the informal interactive hearings?" is a calque — a specialist writes "How long were the informal interactive hearings to run?"; "What legal status applied to X?" is a calque — a specialist writes "Was X lawful ...?" or "Was X contrary to international law ...?". Yes/no questions are welcome and common ("Did the arms embargo on Rwanda cover non-governmental forces in May 1994?", "Was UNMIL's mandate still in force in June 2011?"); their answer is still the span of the block that decides the question, never "yes" or "no".
3. TIME PIN — MANDATORY. Every question carries an explicit absolute time anchor: a date ("as at 30 April 2011"), a month or year ("from May 1994", "in force in 2004"), or a dated act ("under the extension agreed in December 2011", "the measures imposed in May 1994", "extended on 30 June 2006"), taken from the block, the context or the metadata date. Document-relative time is forbidden — "current", "now", "recently", "the day before", "at its next session", "the reporting period", a date without a year: resolve or discard.
ANCHORS: besides the time pin, every question carries at least TWO substantive anchors in its own text, from: the regime or situation ("the arms embargo on Rwanda", "the Iran sanctions regime", "the Biological Weapons Convention"), the country or territory, the mission or body ("UNAMIR", "the Panel of Experts on the Sudan"), the actor bound or protected, or the measure or term of art at issue. The regime must be NAMED: "the Programme of Action" without "small arms and light weapons" fits the Barbados, Istanbul, Almaty and Durban Programmes of Action equally; "victims and witnesses" without "crimes by United Nations officials and experts on mission" is anchorless. Generic actors are not anchors: "States", "Member States", "the Secretary-General", "the Office of the High Commissioner". Every definite description is named in the question itself — never bare "the Committee", "the sides", "the Mission", "the Government". Report the anchors in "anchors" as verbatim substrings of the question; a phrase that appears only in the answer is not an anchor.
THE SIBLING TEST AND RECURRING SERIES — why the pin and the anchors exist: UN norms recur by design. The same mandate is renewed year after year in near-identical words, so "What troop ceiling applied to UNMISS?" has a different answer for every renewal — the time pin picks the year. The same asset-freeze, travel-ban and reporting clauses are cloned across regimes, so "Who was exempt from the travel ban?" fits a dozen regimes — the regime anchor picks the one. Know the recurring families: session-numbered General Assembly resolutions on standing agenda items (human rights in a country, the right to food, the right to development, assistance to Non-Self-Governing Territories, the Biological and Chemical Weapons Conventions, New Caledonia, criminal accountability of UN officials, the rule of law); the annual ECOSOC and Assembly resolutions on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and the occupied Syrian Golan; the biennial "cooperation between the United Nations and [regional organization]" resolutions; the biennial programme-planning and pattern-of-conferences resolutions; mandate renewals; International Day resolutions; monthly and periodic reports. For these, the year alone is not enough when the paragraph is unchanged year to year: ask only about content specific to THIS instance — a date, a figure, a newly added task, a named event. A monthly KFOR report recurs, but its troop figure is this month's own. Before keeping a question ask: would it, word for word, be an equally sensible question about last year's renewal or another regime's twin? If yes, add what is missing, target this instance's content, or skip with skip_reason "recurring boilerplate". Apply the same test to the answer in its question context: recurring wording alone does not distinguish an instance; a short answer remains valid when the question pins down a specific measure, event or figure.
CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT ONLY:
- QUALIFYING spans: measures imposed, extended or terminated; mandate scope and tasks; conditions, criteria, exemptions; deadlines and mandate periods; ceilings, appropriations, contributions, reported figures; appointments, composition, procedures; concrete dated events and determinations.
- DISQUALIFIED spans, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; reaffirms a determination first made elsewhere; reaffirms a request to CONTINUE an activity; encourages or invites in general terms; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; recommends that Governments accord priority; commemorations and anniversaries; aspirations; preambular recitals.
ATTRIBUTION: reports state the reporting body's findings and letters convey positions; a finding or figure stays attributed and dated, to the OFFICE or STATE, never a bare personal name — "According to KFOR's report for February 2007, were any incidents against KFOR recorded in Kosovo?" An agentless passive is stripped attribution: "was proposed", "were recorded", "was reported" without the proposer, recorder or reporter — name the source from the block. The finding must be a figure, event or determination a practitioner would verify, never rhetoric; never present an attributed claim as established fact.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST — the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. Four ways to fail it:
- Restatement: the answer repeats the question's words or the pointer it was built from ("the exemptions established by the Committee" for "what exemptions applied").
- Guessability: a specialist could complete the answer from the question with better than even odds ("one-day" for the duration of informal hearings; "in writing" for the form of a request).
- Answer scaffolding: the question was formed by truncating the answer span and interrogating its tail. Rebuild from the need, not from the span's syntax.
- Deictic answer: the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document — "the above priorities", "as adopted in the present resolution", "the measures set out below". Discard, or narrow to a self-contained span.
CORE RULES:
- Smallest Unit: exactly ONE norm element or fact per question — one deadline, one figure, one criterion, one exemption, one actor, one condition. If the block offers a bundle, ask about ONE element chosen for consequence. Prefer questions whose complete answer is a short span; if the natural answer is a paragraph or a long list, narrow or discard.
- Wording & Length: direct interrogative, 8–20 words, hard maximum 25.
- Diversity: the questions must target different facts; if two or more pairs pass every rule, span at least two categories.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — eight categories ("question_type"), in priority order, each with the norm-state shapes practitioners use for it:
  1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures in force, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "What exemptions applied to [measure] in [year]?", "Under what conditions was [measure] to be reviewed as of [date]?", "Did the arms embargo on [country] cover [actors] in [month year]?"
  2. date_deadline_or_mandate — mandate start, extension and expiry; reporting and compliance deadlines; effective and review dates: "By what date was [actor] required to [X], as of [year]?", "Until when was [mission]'s mandate extended on [date]?", "Was [mission]'s mandate still in force in [month year]?"
  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations, assessed and outstanding contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What troop ceiling applied to [mission] from [month year]?", "What amount of [contributions] was outstanding as at [date]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — reporting duties and frequency, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] required to report on [X] in [year]?", "Who was to verify [X] under [dated act]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, formally defined terms: "Who was responsible for [X] in [year]?", "Which body decided [X] as of [date]?"
  6. situation_scope_or_coverage — what a measure covered: country, territory, population, period, carve-outs: "What did [mission]'s mandate cover from [date]?", "Did [measure] apply to [territory] in [year]?"
  7. operative_action, recast as norm-state — the obligation, task or authorization in force, not the act of deciding it: "What was [party] required to do by [date] under [dated act]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated figures, incidents and determinations, attributed to office or State: "According to [office]'s [month year] report, what was [figure] as at [date]?", "According to [State]'s [month year] letter, did [X] happen?"
Purpose or rationale only when the block states it explicitly and completely.

SELF-CHECK every question, in this order:
1. Unchanged recurring text? A quoted provision of another instrument as the target? → skip or reframe to what this document does with it.
2. No instrument reference — no number, symbol, paragraph number or instrument description as locator; only resolution-named bodies, dated-act pins and office-or-State-plus-date attributions.
3. Norm-state stance, written naturally — no "what did X decide / request / call upon / continue to do / say", no "what duration / status applied" calque; a yes/no question answered by a deciding span.
4. Absolute time pin present; no document-relative time anywhere.
5. Two substantive anchors in the question, regime named, reported verbatim; every definite description named; SIBLING TEST passed, with this instance's own content where the series recurs.
6. Answer span QUALIFYING, not a softer ceremonial form or an annual reaffirmation; finding attributed to office or State, no agentless passive; INFORMATIVENESS passed — no restatement, no guessable answer, no answer scaffolding, no deictic span.
7. BLOCK TEST: answer fully in the block, not from a reference, the context or metadata.
8. One smallest-unit fact; 8–20 words (max 25); terms of art verbatim, paraphrase without drift; figures exact in the answer. Fewer than three passed? Output fewer. None? Output the skip.
