Cooperation with the European Union, meanwhile, had also continued to develop in unprecedented ways, as in the election security assistance the European Union had provided in the Democratic Republic of the Congo or the NATO-led military presence in Kosovo and Afghanistan, where the United Nations had only a civilian presence.
It must focus on two strategic priorities.
9. The first priority was to run the machinery of peacekeeping effectively, with greater professionalism and efficiency, in accordance with the reform programme he had set out the previous year in Peace Operations 2010.
Progress had been made in a number of areas in the past year.
10. 11. Equally essential was the quality and baseline quantity of the military and police personnel so much in demand in recent operations.

12. Effective performance by any peacekeeping personnel, of course, depended on the training they received.
13. A continuing concern was the safety and security of peacekeeping personnel.
14. In the area of doctrine, the Department had now developed a framework for incorporating lessons learned and best practices into actionable policy guidelines.

15. The Department had found that it must implement an integrated team approach within a robust organizational framework to manage its large, decentralized staff.
Following an audit by the Office of Internal Oversight Services, the Department would be formulating concrete proposals to strengthen management capacity and conducting a department-wide review of its business processes.

16. To enhance its culture of accountability, the Department had increased its capacity for early identification of conduct issues.

Guidelines on how to handle cases of misconduct had been circulated in the field, and a system for tracking and investigating cases was in place at Headquarters.

I would like to take this opportunity, on behalf of the Government and the people of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, to convey our most heartfelt condolences to the people of Indonesia in connection with the recent tragedy that has once again struck that country.
I would like to place on record before the Assembly that our delegation will not oppose the draft resolution endorsing the report of the Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations (A/59/19) that was adopted by the Special Political and Decolonization Committee (Fourth Committee).
However, we would like to make the following explanations.

The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela would once again like to make known in the Hall its opinion regarding peacekeeping operations as they are currently constituted in line with the provisions of the Charter of the United Nations.
We reaffirm that we have no objection whatever to peacekeeping operations whose provisions and strict purposes are the maintenance of peace, just as such operations have taken place historically.
A look into the ideological construct underpinning the new type of peacekeeping operations prompts us to make a few observations.
The fact is that the idea of a collapsed, failed or impotent State that is employed as the basis for those new operations is devoid of any historical perspective.
That idea tacitly implies that the collapse of a State is the responsibility of the people and Government that find themselves in that situation.
To the contrary, we know that many States that are today labelled as failed States have been failed States from their very beginnings, as they were in the main created as fronts for what in fact were dependent entities that were economically and politically subordinate neo-colonial foreign protectorates or quasi-protectorates.

[... the TARGET BLOCK appears here ...]

Nor do we accept the excuse of humanitarian intervention or the political use of human rights as grounds for the imposition on any State of enforcement measures falling outside the Charter.
A serious precedent in that regard is the recent proposal by the Secretary-General to grant powers to the Security Council, on the basis of the supposed principle of the responsibility to protect, to punish States for crimes stipulated in the Statute of the International Criminal Court.
We are sufficiently aware of the double standards employed by, and the undeclared goals of, those who have a monopoly on labelling such actions.
United Nations peacekeeping operations are solely a tool to carry out the provisions of the Charter.
In order for that to be a reality, peacekeeping operations must strictly adhere to the principles of the consent of the parties involved, impartiality and non-use of force except in cases strictly pertaining to legitimate self-defence.

The mandates of peacekeeping operations must therefore not be ambiguous, so as to avoid skewing the operation and making it possible for the powers it is given to be usurped by United Nations bodies that have no right to them.
Similarly, peacekeeping operations should have the necessary logistical resources to achieve the desired result of lasting and sustainable peace.
Moreover, peacekeeping operations must not take the place of resolving the real underlying causes of conflict.
They must therefore not be a substitute for addressing the root causes that are usually at the heart of major socio-economic problems.
The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela therefore favours the prevention of conflicts by overcoming the serious problems that lead to instability and to conflict situations, as there can be neither lasting peace nor strengthened democratic institutions without development.
Every decision taken with regard to peacekeeping operations must abide by the fundamental principles of international law as enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. In other words, there must be full respect for sovereignty, non-interference in internal affairs and self-determination for peoples.

That position is based upon the mandate enshrined in the Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, whose preamble commits us to promoting peaceful cooperation between nations and the strengthening of Latin American integration in accordance with the principles of non-intervention, the self-determination of peoples, universal and inalienable guarantees of human rights, democratizing international society, nuclear disarmament, ecological balance and the preservation of legal and environmental well-being as humankind's common undeniable patrimony.
The peacekeeping operation in Haiti deserves special mention.
Venezuela does not support any action that could damage, infringe upon, alter or impair the ultimate right of the Haitian people to take decisions for itself with regard to its future, its social and political institutions and its path to development in order to overcome poverty.
Finally, we cannot fail to refer to the responsibility incumbent upon the Security Council when it decides to carry out a peacekeeping operation.
There will also be doubts as to whether it is possible to intervene in any State -- or just in weak ones.

The President (spoke in French): The Assembly will now take a decision on the draft resolution recommended by the Special Political and Decolonization Committee (Fourth Committee) in paragraph 7 of its report (A/59/472/Add.1).
The Special Political and Decolonization Committee (Fourth Committee) adopted the draft resolution without a vote. May take it that the Assembly wishes to do the same?
The draft resolution was adopted (resolution 59/281).

You are an expert at creating legal retrieval questions from United Nations documents (resolutions, reports, letters, and meeting records).
PRACTITIONER MODE — THE SPECIALIST ASKS FOR THE STATE OF THE LAW, NOT FOR A DOCUMENT: every question is a query from a specialist who works the regime — sanctions counsel, a desk lawyer, a compliance officer, a peacekeeping legal adviser. No instrument is in their head; the NORM is. They ask what applied, who was bound, by when something was due, under what conditions something changed, what a mandate covered, what a figure stood at — at a point in time. The document is merely where the answer lives; the question never uses a document as a locator. A dated report or letter may appear solely to attribute a finding (ATTRIBUTION). The test throughout: would a regime specialist plausibly type roughly these words while advising on compliance, reviewing a mandate, or reconstructing what applied at a given date?
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English. In the ANSWER, reproduce dates, durations, amounts, percentages, troop figures and thresholds exactly. Use the official English names of organs, bodies, missions and instruments, never literal translations.
PARAPHRASE WITHOUT DRIFT: paraphrase the ordinary scaffolding around the norm; never lift multi-word descriptive fragments from the block as question scaffolding, and never reproduce a list the block gives. Copy terms of art and proper nouns exactly ("asset freeze", "safe humanitarian areas", "assessed contributions", "compensated without further action"). A paraphrase must not widen, narrow or shift the norm: "when the Secretary-General compensated an applicant" is not "when the Secretary-General decided the applicant be compensated without further action" — the first describes any payment, the second the specific statutory option the cap attaches to. Legal text is sensitive to exact words — when unsure whether a word is load-bearing, keep it.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document is, WHEN it is from — often the source of your time pin — and whether it belongs to a recurring series.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which parties "the sides" are, which regime a measure belongs to, who wrote the letter or report, the calendar dates that pin the question. If any part of the answer's substance sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument — an article of the Institution-Building Package, a paragraph of an earlier resolution, a rule from a statute — a norm-state question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument, whose own text is the better match in this corpus, so the gold would be wrong; ask instead about what THIS document does with it: what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.
THE DEFINING RULES — NO INSTRUMENT, NORM-STATE STANCE, TIME-PINNED:
1. NO INSTRUMENT REFERENCE. The question contains no resolution or decision number, no document symbol, no paragraph number, and no instrument used as a locator, by identifier or by description: not "under resolution 918 (1994)", not "under the 1994 Security Council resolution on Rwanda", not "under the Secretary-General's May 1994 report, what ceiling applied". If the question cannot be asked without pointing at an instrument, it belongs to the lookup mode — discard it here. Three things are not instrument references: bodies named after resolutions ("the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1533 (2004)", "the 1267 Committee") — a name, not a citation; dated-act time pins (rule 3); and the office-or-State-plus-date attribution of a finding or figure (ATTRIBUTION), which is part of the fact. Identifiers may appear inside the ANSWER span.
2. NORM-STATE STANCE. Ask what applied, was required, was in force, was due — not what an organ said, decided, requested, called for or continued to do. The organ may appear as the actor of the norm; the speech act is never the thing asked about. Banned forms: "What did the Security Council decide / request / authorize / encourage / reaffirm ...", "What were States called upon to consider ...", "What did [body] continue to do ...", "What role did [body] play ...", "What did the resolution say ...". Write the stance naturally: it is a perspective, not a template. "What duration applied to the informal interactive hearings?" is a calque — a specialist writes "How long were the informal interactive hearings to run?"; "What legal status applied to X?" is a calque — a specialist writes "Was X lawful ...?" or "Was X contrary to international law ...?". Yes/no questions are welcome and common ("Did the arms embargo on Rwanda cover non-governmental forces in May 1994?", "Was UNMIL's mandate still in force in June 2011?"); their answer is still the span of the block that decides the question, never "yes" or "no".

The same asset-freeze, travel-ban and reporting clauses are cloned across regimes, so "Who was exempt from the travel ban?" fits a dozen regimes — the regime anchor picks the one. CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT ONLY:
- QUALIFYING spans: measures imposed, extended or terminated; mandate scope and tasks; conditions, criteria, exemptions; deadlines and mandate periods; ceilings, appropriations, contributions, reported figures; appointments, composition, procedures; concrete dated events and determinations.
- DISQUALIFIED spans, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; reaffirms a determination first made elsewhere; reaffirms a request to CONTINUE an activity; encourages or invites in general terms; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; recommends that Governments accord priority; commemorations and anniversaries; aspirations; preambular recitals.
ATTRIBUTION: reports state the reporting body's findings and letters convey positions; a finding or figure stays attributed and dated, to the OFFICE or STATE, never a bare personal name — "According to KFOR's report for February 2007, were any incidents against KFOR recorded in Kosovo?" An agentless passive is stripped attribution: "was proposed", "were recorded", "was reported" without the proposer, recorder or reporter — name the source from the block. The finding must be a figure, event or determination a practitioner would verify, never rhetoric; never present an attributed claim as established fact.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST — the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. Four ways to fail it:
- Restatement: the answer repeats the question's words or the pointer it was built from ("the exemptions established by the Committee" for "what exemptions applied").
- Guessability: a specialist could complete the answer from the question with better than even odds ("one-day" for the duration of informal hearings; "in writing" for the form of a request).
- Answer scaffolding: the question was formed by truncating the answer span and interrogating its tail. Rebuild from the need, not from the span's syntax.
- Deictic answer: the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document — "the above priorities", "as adopted in the present resolution", "the measures set out below". Discard, or narrow to a self-contained span.
CORE RULES:
- Smallest Unit: exactly ONE norm element or fact per question — one deadline, one figure, one criterion, one exemption, one actor, one condition. If the block offers a bundle, ask about ONE element chosen for consequence. Prefer questions whose complete answer is a short span; if the natural answer is a paragraph or a long list, narrow or discard.
- Wording & Length: direct interrogative, 8–20 words, hard maximum 25.
- Diversity: the questions must target different facts; if two or more pairs pass every rule, span at least two categories.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — eight categories ("question_type"), in priority order, each with the norm-state shapes practitioners use for it:
  1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures in force, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "What exemptions applied to [measure] in [year]?", "Under what conditions was [measure] to be reviewed as of [date]?", "Did the arms embargo on [country] cover [actors] in [month year]?"
  2. date_deadline_or_mandate — mandate start, extension and expiry; reporting and compliance deadlines; effective and review dates: "By what date was [actor] required to [X], as of [year]?", "Until when was [mission]'s mandate extended on [date]?", "Was [mission]'s mandate still in force in [month year]?"
  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations, assessed and outstanding contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What troop ceiling applied to [mission] from [month year]?", "What amount of [contributions] was outstanding as at [date]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — reporting duties and frequency, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] required to report on [X] in [year]?", "Who was to verify [X] under [dated act]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, formally defined terms: "Who was responsible for [X] in [year]?", "Which body decided [X] as of [date]?"
  6. situation_scope_or_coverage — what a measure covered: country, territory, population, period, carve-outs: "What did [mission]'s mandate cover from [date]?", "Did [measure] apply to [territory] in [year]?"
  7. operative_action, recast as norm-state — the obligation, task or authorization in force, not the act of deciding it: "What was [party] required to do by [date] under [dated act]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated figures, incidents and determinations, attributed to office or State: "According to [office]'s [month year] report, what was [figure] as at [date]?", "According to [State]'s [month year] letter, did [X] happen?"
Purpose or rationale only when the block states it explicitly and completely.

✗ "What was the current ceiling for the least developed countries' rate of assessment?" → "current" is document-relative. Fix: "What ceiling applied to the least developed countries' rate of assessment in 2005?"
SELF-CHECK every question, in this order:
1. Unchanged recurring text? A quoted provision of another instrument as the target? → skip or reframe to what this document does with it.
2. No instrument reference — no number, symbol, paragraph number or instrument description as locator; only resolution-named bodies, dated-act pins and office-or-State-plus-date attributions.
3. Norm-state stance, written naturally — no "what did X decide / request / call upon / continue to do / say", no "what duration / status applied" calque; a yes/no question answered by a deciding span.
4. Absolute time pin present; no document-relative time anywhere.
5. Two substantive anchors in the question, regime named, reported verbatim; every definite description named; SIBLING TEST passed, with this instance's own content where the series recurs.
6. Answer span QUALIFYING, not a softer ceremonial form or an annual reaffirmation; finding attributed to office or State, no agentless passive; INFORMATIVENESS passed — no restatement, no guessable answer, no answer scaffolding, no deictic span.
7. BLOCK TEST: answer fully in the block, not from a reference, the context or metadata.
8. One smallest-unit fact; 8–20 words (max 25); terms of art verbatim, paraphrase without drift; figures exact in the answer. Fewer than three passed? Output fewer. None? Output the skip.

44. The Government was concerned by the high unemployment rate among women.
To some extent the figures were skewed by the fact that the long-term unemployed were not dropped from the count.
There had been a reduction in some types of female unemployment over the past two years.
Like the other European countries, Belgium had a national employment plan that aimed at employment for all but placed special emphasis on quality jobs.
Many of the measures under that plan were particularly relevant to women, because they specifically targeted the long-term, the older and the low-skilled unemployed.
45. Ms. Verzele (Belgium) said that the project of removing inequalities from the tax system was still ongoing; the Ministry of Finance was studying the matter carefully and there would undoubtedly be more information to give in the next report.
With regard to development aid, Belgium was a staunch advocate of equality of opportunity.
The communities and regions had sole responsibility for education, but it should be understood that they, as well as the Federal Government, had to approve international treaties before they could be ratified by Belgium, so that they were also committed to implementing the treaty provisions.
Although no representative of the German-speaking community was present, it had contributed to the report.

Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women
Twenty-seventh session
Summary record of the 560th meeting
Held at Headquarters, New York, on Monday, 10 June 2002, at 3 p.m.
Chairperson: Ms. Acar (Vice-Chairperson)

Consideration of reports submitted by States parties under article 18 of the Convention (continued)
Combined third and fourth periodic reports of Belgium (continued)
In the absence of Ms. Abaka, Ms. Acar, Vice-Chairperson, took the Chair.

1. At the invitation of the Chairperson, Ms. Adriaenssens, Ms. Franken, Ms. Paternottre, Ms. Stevens and Ms. Verzele (Belgium) took places at the Committee table.
The position of the Minister for Equal Opportunities near the top of the federal hierarchy gave added impetus to the process.
Various initiatives by the regions and communities would be described later.
The Parliament elected in 1999 had established an inter-ministerial conference on literacy, which would deal with the literacy problems of migrant women.
In response to Ms. Manalo's question, she said that the French-speaking community was coordinating the gender equality activities of its various ministries, and had formulated a plan on equal opportunities and submitted proposals to the Government to that end.
The Equal Opportunities Service of the French-speaking community operated on a budget of 756,000 euros, but specific projects were financed by the ministries concerned.
The training of female executives would not happen overnight but was a long-term process.

4. She did not have figures available on the number of women in high-level posts in the press, or on female members of the Senior Audio-Visual Council.
She would provide that information in writing, together with statistical information on the implementation of the code of ethics adopted in 1994 by various French-speaking television stations.
She believed there had been a misunderstanding with regard to gender mainstreaming in the Flemish community, which had been the first to launch mainstreaming efforts following the Fourth World Conference on Women, held in Beijing.
The community had set up the Interdepartmental Commission on Equal Opportunities, and mainstreaming initiatives of the various departments were coordinated by the Equal Opportunities Unit in Flanders. It was not always an easy task; a delicate balance had to be struck between urging the various ministries to ensure mainstreaming within their own areas of competence and respecting their autonomy.
The budget had grown exponentially, from 120,000 euros in 1995 to 4.3 million euros in 2002.
The Equal Opportunities Unit in Flanders did not work with women exclusively but rather targeted a number of other vulnerable groups as well, including migrants, disabled persons and children.

6. Various mainstreaming instruments had been developed, including legislation establishing quotas and mandating implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action and a questionnaire which set out fundamental considerations for policy-making from a gender perspective.
A local gender impact assessment instrument had been developed two years later in 1999, on the basis of lessons learned from the original questionnaire.
7. She agreed that perhaps the report emphasized implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action at the expense of the Convention itself.
That was partly because of the legislation on implementing the Beijing Platform and partly because the Platform outlined clear and practical strategic goals for the Government, non-governmental organizations and other entities.
Her Unit would make every effort to compensate for giving insufficient coverage to the implementation of the Convention.
8. Turning to Committee members' questions on migrant women, she said that the Flemish community was responsible for receiving migrants, finding shelter for them and helping them adapt to their new life.
The Equal Opportunities Unit had established an organization to coordinate actions by all migrant women, from various ethnic groups.
Studies showed that second- and third-generation migrant girls performed better in school than boys but that many did not pursue a higher education.

In 1999, the Equal Opportunities Unit had launched a project, in conjunction with institutions of higher learning, to increase the number of migrant girls in higher education.
A separate hotline had been set up for migrant women in need of assistance.
9. Replying to the question concerning the Unit's relationship with non-governmental organizations, she said that the Women's Council, which coordinated the work of the various women's organizations in the Flemish community, was allocated resources from her Unit's annual budget.
The Unit had also conducted a workshop for the six existing Flemish women's organizations to obtain their input and offer them guidance where necessary.
Every effort was made to encourage the media to help transform mentalities without violating constitutional freedoms.
An impact assessment of gender mainstreaming in the media would be completed by the end of the year.
Zorra, an organization that acted as a watchdog for advertising and the media, had organized an e-mail forum for receiving complaints and attempted to discourage advertisers from publicizing sexist material.
She would give the Committee statistics on female journalists in a written response.

11. Ms. Verzele (Belgium) pointed out that communauté flamande should be translated as Flemish community, not Walloon community.
12. Ms. Livingstone Raday cautioned against using mediation to deal with violence against women, as it put pressure on the victims and perpetuated the problem by forcing all parties to compromise.
She wondered whether the State party recognized that danger and had taken measures to offset it, for example, by restricting mediation to first-time offenders, or to offences where physical violence or psychological abuse had not been serious.
She also wondered whether victims were provided with an independent advocate to represent them in proceedings.
13. Ms. Gaspard hailed the State party's introduction of legislation to increase the number of female candidates for elective office but noted that the number actually elected had not necessarily increased and that, in certain cases, even the minimum quota of candidates had not been met.
She would appreciate a progress report on the revision of the progressive 1994 law promoting parity in electoral lists and stressed that, beyond participation in political life, women must also be integrated into the civil service and the advisory bodies, which played a strategic role in government.

She wondered whether a 1990 law (revised in 1997) to increase the number of females on those advisory bodies was being properly implemented and what other measures the State party could take to that end.
14. Referring to article 8, she expressed concern at the decline in the number of women taking the foreign service entrance examination and wondered what action would be taken to remedy the situation.
15. Ms. Achmad said that she fully supported Ms. Gaspard's remarks and shared her concern.
She wondered how the Belgian Government would ensure the sustainability of its affirmative action policies to increase women's participation in political life.
Was it taking measures to ensure that leaders in Government, political parties and trade unions complied with the State party's obligations under the Convention?
She echoed previous speakers' concern that the report did not focus on the Convention as the primary instrument to promote equality.

Although such facilities constituted major support for female diplomats, she hoped that they would also be a means of encouraging men to shoulder a greater share of the responsibilities of family life.
She praised the State party's approach to dealing with the media through dialogue and suggestion; perhaps that same approach would be effective with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and even non-governmental organizations and labour unions.
17. Ms. Kapalata agreed wholeheartedly with Ms. Gaspard's questions and comments concerning articles 7 and 8.
She welcomed the introduction of a quota system, which was a step in the right direction, and hoped that it would be extended to all levels of government. The report seemed to imply, under article 8, that it would take some time for female diplomats to attain the status necessary to become head of post.
She called for special measures to expedite the process and hoped to see tangible results in the State party's next report.

18. Ms. Tavares da Silva asked whether there had been any provisions in the former electoral law to ensure that women candidates were not relegated to the lower places on electoral lists, and whether there had been any investigation as to why the number of women taking part in entrance examinations for the diplomatic service had declined sharply in recent years and what barriers women might be facing in that regard.
19. She added that the Beijing Platform for Action and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women were complementary; the former was a legal text, and the latter a policy document.
20. Ms. Manalo asked what was the policy in relation to situations where spouses were employed in the career diplomatic service, whether both partners were encouraged to continue their careers, and what was the situation when one of them was required to take up a foreign posting.

21. Ms. Verzele (Belgium) said that her delegation agreed with Ms. Tavares da Silva as to the respective roles of the Beijing Platform for Action and the Convention.
22. Her Government was well aware that gender equality should be a concern for men as well as women, and awareness and involvement by men must be improved, particularly in respect of family activities.
23. The 1994 law on gender quotas on electoral lists applied to the composition of the lists themselves; it did not require that a particular result should be achieved. Given the functioning of the system of electoral lists under the Belgian system of proportional representation, candidates whose names appeared at the top of the list were more likely to be elected.
It was also true that, owing to regional peculiarities, it was more difficult for women candidates to be successful in the Walloon region.
24. On 30 May 2002, a new electoral law had been adopted.
It would require that 50 per cent of candidates should be women and that men and women candidates should alternate in the first and second places at the top of each list; furthermore, that legislation did not include any transitional provisions.

She drew the Committee's attention to the information on page 39 of the English-language text of her delegation's responses to the list of issues, concerning the composition of advisory bodies: about 28 per cent of the positions involved were now occupied by women.
As for the decline in the numbers of women seeking to enter the diplomatic service, plans were being prepared for information campaigns to improve awareness among young women of the opportunities available to them; the Government also planned to increase the proportion of women on the juries for the corresponding entrance examinations.
25. Ms. Stevens (Belgium) said that the measures taken by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to improve the representation of women in the diplomatic service included a day-care centre and the availability of a Family Officer.
These services were available for use by both women and men.
Research was being undertaken to determine whether the fall in the numbers of women seeking to enter the diplomatic service might have been influenced by developments in the labour market as a whole.
As for the position of spouses in the diplomatic service, she was not aware that there had ever been an attempt to discourage the spouse of a diplomatic officer from remaining in employment.

A working group was looking into ways of helping the spouses of diplomatic officials posted abroad to continue to work; bilateral agreements with receiving States were one means of achieving that.
26. Ms. Paternottre (Belgium) said that steps had been taken to contact young women who had attended briefings on diplomatic careers but had decided not to take the entrance examinations, in order to determine the reasons for their decision.
One reason was that young women desiring a diplomatic career seldom had a spouse who did not work.
It would, however, be very difficult to explain why there were fewer women candidates in a specific year.
27. Responding to an earlier question relating to family mediation, she said that it was an experiment being conducted in the Brussels region.
When the police were called to deal with a problem of domestic violence, they asked the two partners whether they wished to avail themselves of a mediation service.
The mediation was offered not as an alternative to the usual investigation and prosecution but as a parallel, complementary service.

The first phase had involved invoking the federal legislation to increase the numbers of women candidates on electoral lists; the second phase had involved encouraging the public to vote for women candidates; and the third phase, implemented after the elections, had focused on political leaders, seeking to persuade them to give decision-making positions to women who had been elected.
The number of women candidates elected had increased to 27 per cent, an improvement of seven percentage points over the previous elections, and there had been an increase in the numbers of women given executive mandates.
29. To follow up those achievements, a strategic plan had been established, consisting of two tracks: the first to empower women who had been elected, so that they were not left out of decision-making processes, and the second to prepare more women to become candidates in future elections.
A project had been set up for the mentoring of women candidates who had been elected to the Community Councils, and a gender training course for politicians was being made available by a non-governmental organization.
The influence of the media was also being used: press conferences with political leaders in Flanders were being organized, at which they were asked to explain what they were doing to empower women and increase the numbers of women candidates.

An instrument known as the "family and business audit" was being developed to enable employers to determine how "family-friendly" their organizations were; it would be ready by the end of 2002, and it was hoped that it would help to improve awareness.
Articles 10 to14 30. Ms. Corti congratulated the reporting State on its health policies, particularly regarding HIV/AIDS.
Recalling that the Committee had been informed that the problems of elderly women were the object of much debate in Belgium, she asked which specific aspects were being considered; in particular, she wished to know what measures and institutions existed to deal with the problem of solitude among older women; with the increase in life expectancy, the scale of that problem was growing.
31. Ms. Abaka expressed concerned at the apparent lack of uniformity in compliance with obligations under the Convention, particularly in the area of health, in the country's different regions.
She also wondered who spoke for the inhabitants of the German-speaking area and of the Brussels region, and whether there was an independent body in Belgium which could coordinate all aspects of human rights throughout the country.

"### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document is, when it is from and whether it belongs to a recurring series; the subject-matter words of its title ("the situation in Rwanda") may serve as topic words in a question.

If any needed fact, figure, list or reason sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument, a question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument; ask instead about what THIS document does with it — what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.

1. NO IDENTIFIERS: no resolution or decision number, document symbol or paragraph number in a question, and no deixis — "this resolution", "the present report", "this document", the document's contents as if visible. Identifiers may appear inside the answer span.

Ask about the situation, the response or the affected party itself; what attributed content may be asked about, and how, is set out under ATTRIBUTION.
LEXICAL DISTANCE — the retriever must match on meaning, not keyword overlap. Distance comes from describing the SITUATION, RESPONSE or PEOPLE in ordinary words instead of the document's formulas — "the mass killing of civilians" for "the very numerous killings of civilians"; "UN peacekeepers" for the mission's formal designation; "people who fled across the border" for "refugees who crossed the border" — and never from lifting the block's phrasing or reproducing a list it gives. Distance must NOT come from renaming terms of art or official names: "arms embargo" is not "weapons ban", "asset freeze" is not "account blocking"; an International Day, a body, a mission keeps its name (an official acronym may be expanded). A substituted term changes what is being asked about; legal and diplomatic text is sensitive to exact words — when unsure whether a word is load-bearing, keep it. Paraphrase never strips the discriminating anchor: keep the country, the mission and the year.
ANCHOR — the person typing has not seen this document and is searching among hundreds of thousands of UN documents in the same formulaic register. Every question carries at least one concrete anchor: a country or situation ("Rwanda", "the conflict in Darfur"), a mission or operation ("UNAMIR"), a named body or actor type ("the Panel of Experts on the Sudan", "troop-contributing countries"), or a subject matter tied to a situation ("arms embargo exemptions for humanitarian equipment in Somalia"). A bare topic ("counterterrorism measures", "climate action", "developing countries", "human rights learning") is not an anchor. Every definite description is named in the question itself — never bare "the Committee", "the Regional Centre", "the speaker", "the sides", "the Council". Report the anchor in "anchor" as a verbatim substring of the question. The test: typed into a search engine by a stranger, would the question lead to THIS document's subject matter? "What did the Security Council express grave concern about?" fails; "How did the Security Council respond to attacks on displaced civilians in Rwanda in May 1994?" passes.
RECURRING SERIES — know the families: session-numbered General Assembly resolutions on standing agenda items (a country's human rights situation, the right to food, the right to development, human rights learning, the Chemical and Biological Weapons Conventions, New Caledonia); the annual ECOSOC and Assembly resolutions on the Occupied Palestinian Territory; the biennial "cooperation between the United Nations and [regional organization]" resolutions, whose consultation clauses are cloned across the OSCE, CIS, SCO, EurAsEC and every other partner; mandate renewals; International Day resolutions; periodic reports. An unchanged paragraph in such a series fits every year — and every partner organization — equally, even with the year attached; the same holds for any span that could appear unchanged in dozens of UN documents (stakeholder invitation lists, cooperate-and-collaborate lists, the universal "measures must comply with international law" clause, "primary responsibility lies with the authorities themselves"). Ask only about content specific to THIS instance — a named event, a new task, a figure; if the block holds only unchanged recurring text, skip with skip_reason "recurring boilerplate". When a block holds both ceremony and substance, ask about the substance.
CONSEQUENTIAL ANSWER SPANS:
- QUALIFYING: measures established, extended or modified; mandates and their scope; conditions, criteria and exemptions; how a mechanism operates; who is bound, protected or assisted and how; concrete reported events, findings and stated rationales; and, for situation-framed questions, preambular ASSESSMENTS that state concretely what is happening ("delays by the signatory parties and the absence of an inclusive political settlement", "an estimated 250,000 refugees crossed the border").
- DISQUALIFIED, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; encourages or invites in general terms; invites two officials to hold regular consultations; calls upon bodies to support, cooperate and collaborate with stakeholders; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; aspirations. Preambular RECITALS — recalling, reaffirming, recognizing responsibility, expressing concern — are framing, not answer material, even though preambular ASSESSMENTS are.
ATTRIBUTION — much of this corpus reports what someone SAID. When the block attributes a statement, claim, estimate or assessment, the question and answer preserve the attribution — to the STATE, the OFFICE ("the representative of South Africa", "the Secretary-General"), or, for a Secretariat report, "UN reporting" — never a bare personal name. An agentless passive or a claim stated as fact is stripped attribution: "as weapons kept reaching the separatists" presents Georgia's assertion as fact — write "according to Georgia" or "in Georgia's account". Attributed content is askable only as a State's position on an identifiable proposal, instrument or measure ("What position did Guyana take on the use of force in Kosovo in 1999?"), a stated rationale, or a concrete situation assessment — never a characterization ("how did Guyana describe the crisis"), an aspiration, a courtesy or a generic exhortation. OWN ACTS NEED NO HEDGE: a concrete, completed act of the author's own side — France's letter recounting that the European Union adopted a disarmament plan endorsed by its Heads of State — may be asked about directly; the requirement targets contested claims and characterizations of others.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST: the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. It fails when the answer restates the question's words or the pointer it was built from, when a reader could guess it from the question with better than even odds, or when the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document ("the above priorities", "as adopted in the present resolution"). Discard, or ask about the substance instead.
CORE RULES:
- Single Intent, Short Span: one clear informational goal per question — broader than a single fact is fine, bundled asks are not — answered by a short contiguous span of the block; if the only span is a whole paragraph, narrow the question or discard.
- Wording & Length: natural search phrasing, 8–20 words, hard maximum 25.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — three framings ("framing"); the questions must target distinguishable aspects and, when generating more than one pair, span at least two of them:
  1. situation — context or problem: what crisis, threat, dispute or development does the document respond to or describe? The motivating concern behind a measure, and the state of affairs a report or preamble concretely assesses.
  2. response — mechanism or action: what mission, measure, process or institutional arrangement is established, extended or modified, and how does it operate?
  3. stakeholder — affected party or scenario: who is bound, sanctioned, protected or assisted, and in what real-world scenario? Addressee ("What was the Government of X required to do ...") and beneficiary ("What protection did the UN provide for civilians in ...") perspectives both belong here, as does a State's position on a concrete matter.

44. The Government was concerned by the high unemployment rate among women.
To some extent the figures were skewed by the fact that the long-term unemployed were not dropped from the count.
There had been a reduction in some types of female unemployment over the past two years.
Like the other European countries, Belgium had a national employment plan that aimed at employment for all but placed special emphasis on quality jobs.
Many of the measures under that plan were particularly relevant to women, because they specifically targeted the long-term, the older and the low-skilled unemployed.
45. Ms. Verzele (Belgium) said that the project of removing inequalities from the tax system was still ongoing; the Ministry of Finance was studying the matter carefully and there would undoubtedly be more information to give in the next report.

The communities and regions had sole responsibility for education, but it should be understood that they, as well as the Federal Government, had to approve international treaties before they could be ratified by Belgium, so that they were also committed to implementing the treaty provisions.

Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women
Twenty-seventh session
Summary record of the 560th meeting
Held at Headquarters, New York, on Monday, 10 June 2002, at 3 p.m.
Chairperson: Ms. Acar (Vice-Chairperson)

Consideration of reports submitted by States parties under article 18 of the Convention (continued)
Combined third and fourth periodic reports of Belgium (continued)
In the absence of Ms. Abaka, Ms. Acar, Vice-Chairperson, took the Chair.

1. At the invitation of the Chairperson, Ms. Adriaenssens, Ms. Franken, Ms. Paternottre, Ms. Stevens and Ms. Verzele (Belgium) took places at the Committee table.
The position of the Minister for Equal Opportunities near the top of the federal hierarchy gave added impetus to the process.
Various initiatives by the regions and communities would be described later.
The Parliament elected in 1999 had established an inter-ministerial conference on literacy, which would deal with the literacy problems of migrant women.
In response to Ms. Manalo's question, she said that the French-speaking community was coordinating the gender equality activities of its various ministries, and had formulated a plan on equal opportunities and submitted proposals to the Government to that end.
The Equal Opportunities Service of the French-speaking community operated on a budget of 756,000 euros, but specific projects were financed by the ministries concerned.
The training of female executives would not happen overnight but was a long-term process.

4. She did not have figures available on the number of women in high-level posts in the press, or on female members of the Senior Audio-Visual Council.
She would provide that information in writing, together with statistical information on the implementation of the code of ethics adopted in 1994 by various French-speaking television stations.
She believed there had been a misunderstanding with regard to gender mainstreaming in the Flemish community, which had been the first to launch mainstreaming efforts following the Fourth World Conference on Women, held in Beijing.
The community had set up the Interdepartmental Commission on Equal Opportunities, and mainstreaming initiatives of the various departments were coordinated by the Equal Opportunities Unit in Flanders. It was not always an easy task; a delicate balance had to be struck between urging the various ministries to ensure mainstreaming within their own areas of competence and respecting their autonomy.
The budget had grown exponentially, from 120,000 euros in 1995 to 4.3 million euros in 2002.
The Equal Opportunities Unit in Flanders did not work with women exclusively but rather targeted a number of other vulnerable groups as well, including migrants, disabled persons and children.

6. Various mainstreaming instruments had been developed, including legislation establishing quotas and mandating implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action and a questionnaire which set out fundamental considerations for policy-making from a gender perspective.
A local gender impact assessment instrument had been developed two years later in 1999, on the basis of lessons learned from the original questionnaire.
7. She agreed that perhaps the report emphasized implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action at the expense of the Convention itself.
That was partly because of the legislation on implementing the Beijing Platform and partly because the Platform outlined clear and practical strategic goals for the Government, non-governmental organizations and other entities.
Her Unit would make every effort to compensate for giving insufficient coverage to the implementation of the Convention.
8. Turning to Committee members' questions on migrant women, she said that the Flemish community was responsible for receiving migrants, finding shelter for them and helping them adapt to their new life.
The Equal Opportunities Unit had established an organization to coordinate actions by all migrant women, from various ethnic groups.
Studies showed that second- and third-generation migrant girls performed better in school than boys but that many did not pursue a higher education.

In 1999, the Equal Opportunities Unit had launched a project, in conjunction with institutions of higher learning, to increase the number of migrant girls in higher education.
A separate hotline had been set up for migrant women in need of assistance.
9. Replying to the question concerning the Unit's relationship with non-governmental organizations, she said that the Women's Council, which coordinated the work of the various women's organizations in the Flemish community, was allocated resources from her Unit's annual budget.
The Unit had also conducted a workshop for the six existing Flemish women's organizations to obtain their input and offer them guidance where necessary.
Every effort was made to encourage the media to help transform mentalities without violating constitutional freedoms.
An impact assessment of gender mainstreaming in the media would be completed by the end of the year.
Zorra, an organization that acted as a watchdog for advertising and the media, had organized an e-mail forum for receiving complaints and attempted to discourage advertisers from publicizing sexist material.
She would give the Committee statistics on female journalists in a written response.

11. Ms. Verzele (Belgium) pointed out that communauté flamande should be translated as Flemish community, not Walloon community.
12. Ms. Livingstone Raday cautioned against using mediation to deal with violence against women, as it put pressure on the victims and perpetuated the problem by forcing all parties to compromise.
She wondered whether the State party recognized that danger and had taken measures to offset it, for example, by restricting mediation to first-time offenders, or to offences where physical violence or psychological abuse had not been serious.
She also wondered whether victims were provided with an independent advocate to represent them in proceedings.
13. Ms. Gaspard hailed the State party's introduction of legislation to increase the number of female candidates for elective office but noted that the number actually elected had not necessarily increased and that, in certain cases, even the minimum quota of candidates had not been met.
She would appreciate a progress report on the revision of the progressive 1994 law promoting parity in electoral lists and stressed that, beyond participation in political life, women must also be integrated into the civil service and the advisory bodies, which played a strategic role in government.

She wondered whether a 1990 law (revised in 1997) to increase the number of females on those advisory bodies was being properly implemented and what other measures the State party could take to that end.
14. Referring to article 8, she expressed concern at the decline in the number of women taking the foreign service entrance examination and wondered what action would be taken to remedy the situation.
15. Ms. Achmad said that she fully supported Ms. Gaspard's remarks and shared her concern.
She wondered how the Belgian Government would ensure the sustainability of its affirmative action policies to increase women's participation in political life.

She echoed previous speakers' concern that the report did not focus on the Convention as the primary instrument to promote equality.

Although such facilities constituted major support for female diplomats, she hoped that they would also be a means of encouraging men to shoulder a greater share of the responsibilities of family life.

Ms. Tavares da Silva asked whether there had been any provisions in the former electoral law to ensure that women candidates were not relegated to the lower places on electoral lists, and whether there had been any investigation as to why the number of women taking part in entrance examinations for the diplomatic service had declined sharply in recent years and what barriers women might be facing in that regard.
19. She added that the Beijing Platform for Action and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women were complementary; the former was a legal text, and the latter a policy document.

22. Her Government was well aware that gender equality should be a concern for men as well as women, and awareness and involvement by men must be improved, particularly in respect of family activities.

25. Ms. Stevens (Belgium) said that the measures taken by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to improve the representation of women in the diplomatic service included a day-care centre and the availability of a Family Officer.
These services were available for use by both women and men.
Research was being undertaken to determine whether the fall in the numbers of women seeking to enter the diplomatic service might have been influenced by developments in the labour market as a whole.

26. Ms. Paternottre (Belgium) said that steps had been taken to contact young women who had attended briefings on diplomatic careers but had decided not to take the entrance examinations, in order to determine the reasons for their decision.

It would, however, be very difficult to explain why there were fewer women candidates in a specific year.

When the police were called to deal with a problem of domestic violence, they asked the two partners whether they wished to avail themselves of a mediation service.
The mediation was offered not as an alternative to the usual investigation and prosecution but as a parallel, complementary service.

The first phase had involved invoking the federal legislation to increase the numbers of women candidates on electoral lists; the second phase had involved encouraging the public to vote for women candidates; and the third phase, implemented after the elections, had focused on political leaders, seeking to persuade them to give decision-making positions to women who had been elected.
The number of women candidates elected had increased to 27 per cent, an improvement of seven percentage points over the previous elections, and there had been an increase in the numbers of women given executive mandates.
29. To follow up those achievements, a strategic plan had been established, consisting of two tracks: the first to empower women who had been elected, so that they were not left out of decision-making processes, and the second to prepare more women to become candidates in future elections.
A project had been set up for the mentoring of women candidates who had been elected to the Community Councils, and a gender training course for politicians was being made available by a non-governmental organization.
The influence of the media was also being used: press conferences with political leaders in Flanders were being organized, at which they were asked to explain what they were doing to empower women and increase the numbers of women candidates.

An instrument known as the "family and business audit" was being developed to enable employers to determine how "family-friendly" their organizations were; it would be ready by the end of 2002, and it was hoped that it would help to improve awareness.

You are an expert at creating legal and policy retrieval questions from United Nations documents (resolutions, reports, letters, and meeting records).
LOOKUP MODE — THE PRACTITIONER KNOWS THE INSTRUMENT AND WANTS ONE POINT FROM IT: every question is a query a practitioner — a sanctions-compliance lawyer, a legal adviser, a mission planner, a policy analyst — puts to a search system when they know WHICH instrument or source governs and need ONE precise fact from it: a measure, a deadline, a ceiling, a criterion, a mandate task, a reported figure. Write from the need, not from the text: a working question whose answer happens to live in this passage, never a comprehension question about what the passage says.
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English. In the ANSWER, reproduce dates, durations, amounts, percentages, troop figures, thresholds and identifiers exactly ("within 30 days" stays "within 30 days"). Use the official English names of organs, bodies, missions and instruments, never literal translations.

Copy terms of art, proper names, figures and dates exactly. Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites, each as symbol, title and text. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document IS — organ, type (resolution, decision, report, letter, working paper, meeting record), date — and what it is about.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which parties "the sides" are, which committee "the Committee" is, what a cited instrument is, the organ, type, date and identifier of this document. No identifier of any kind in this rendering. When same-year instruments share a situation, the subject words must pick THIS one out — "the 2011 Security Council resolution establishing the no-fly zone over Libya", not "the 2011 Security Council resolution on Libya".
- DESCRIPTION ACCURACY: describe the instrument AS IT IS, from the metadata — adopting organ and document type, never omitted ("the 2008 resolution on ..." is incomplete: whose?). A letter is described by date, sender and subject ("the 28 July 2014 letter from Israel on the special session"), with the addressee added when the sender wrote more than one letter on the subject — never "the Security Council letter". CORE RULES:
- Single Focus, Smallest Unit: exactly ONE piece of information per question — one deadline, one figure, one criterion, one exemption, one actor. If the block offers a bundle, ask about ONE element chosen for consequence. Prefer questions whose complete answer is a short span; if the natural answer is a paragraph or a long list, narrow or discard.
- Wording & Length: direct interrogative, 8–20 words per rendering, hard maximum 25.
- Diversity: the questions must target different facts and, when generating more than one pair, span at least two categories.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — eight categories ("question_type"), in priority order, each with the shapes practitioners use for it:
  1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures imposed, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "Which measures did the Security Council impose on [regime] in [instrument]?", "Under what condition was [X] to be [Y] under [instrument]?", "Did [instrument] extend the arms embargo on [regime] to [actors]?"
  2. date_deadline_or_mandate — mandate start, extension, expiry; reporting and compliance deadlines; effective and review dates: "By what date was [actor] to [X] under [instrument]?", "Until when did [instrument] extend [mission]'s mandate?"
  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations and contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What force level did the Security Council authorize for [mission] in [instrument]?", "What amount was appropriated for [X] in [instrument]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — who reports to whom and how often, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] to report to the Security Council on [X] under [instrument]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — named officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, defined terms: "Which body was tasked with [X] in [instrument]?" — never the identity of a briefer or speaker, which no practitioner needs.
  6. operative_action — what the organ decides, authorizes, demands or requests, and of whom, when it qualifies under CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT: "What did the Security Council demand of [party] in [instrument]?"
  7. situation_scope_or_coverage — which country, territory, population or period a measure or report covers; carve-outs: "Did [instrument] cover [territory / population]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated facts and conclusions, attributed, only facts a practitioner would verify: "According to [described report], what was [figure] as at [date]?" — cited form "According to the Secretary-General's report S/1999/746, ...".
Yes/no questions are welcome and common; their answer is still the span of the block that decides the question, never "yes" or "no". A bare slot ("What was to be considered ...?", "What did the Assembly request ...?" with no named subject) is not a question.
EXAMPLES — canonical good, both renderings, with the block text they come from:
Target block: S/RES/918 (1994), adopted 17 May 1994: "3. Decides to expand the mandate of UNAMIR to include the protection of displaced persons, refugees and civilians at risk in Rwanda ...; 4. Authorizes in this context an expansion of the UNAMIR force level up to 5,500 troops;"

  → Word-identical outside the slot; the organ acts, the instrument locates; the description carries organ + year + subject and picks 918 out among the 1994 Rwanda resolutions; the anchor sits outside the slot.

The requirements set out in the resolution have not yet been fully met." Reference supplied: S/RES/1559 (2004), listing the requirements.

REAL FAILURES FROM PREVIOUS RUNS — never reproduce these patterns:
✗ "What anniversary was the Office of the High Commissioner asked to continue commemorating in 2011 under the 2011 General Assembly resolution on the right to development?" — answer "the twentyfifth anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development" → the span is "Reaffirms the request ... to continue the commemoration" (DISQUALIFIED); the series is annual and the paragraph recurs; the answer is guessable. Fix: "Under the 1998 General Assembly resolution on human rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, what access to detainees was the ICRC to have?" / "Under A/RES/53/160, what access to detainees was the ICRC to have?"
✗ "From whom may indigenous peoples access financial and technical assistance under the 2006 General Assembly declaration on indigenous peoples?" → description error: A/RES/61/178 is the 2006 resolution deferring consideration of the draft Declaration; there is no "2006 General Assembly declaration".

✗ "Under the 2008 resolution on criminal accountability of United Nations officials and experts on mission, what indication should the Secretary-General request from those States?" → "those States" is unresolved, the organ is missing from the description, and the answer bundles two requests. ✗ "According to CARICOM in A/C.2/58/SR.18, what was South-South cooperation considered to be in relation to a global cooperation system?" → a rhetorical target with no concrete fact or operational or legal effect. Skip.
✗ "In the General Assembly resolution on effects of atomic radiation, what did the Assembly request the Scientific Committee to do at its next session?" → undated description, document-relative time, comprehension frame. Fix: "Under the 2001 General Assembly resolution on the effects of atomic radiation, by which session was UNSCEAR to report its review of ionizing radiation?"
✗ "Which countries did one group of the Panel of Experts on the sanctions regime relating to the Islamic Republic of Iran visit from 10 to 14 September to meet with relevant Government officials on issues related to its mandate?" → a date without a year, lifted filler, 38 words. Fix: "Which countries did the Panel of Experts on the Iran sanctions regime visit in September 2012?"
SELF-CHECK every question, in this order:
1. Unchanged recurring text? A quoted provision of another instrument as the target? → skip or reframe to what this document does with it.
2. RENDERINGS: "question" identifier-free, its description organ + year + subject, type as the metadata gives it, distinguishing same-year siblings; "question_cited" the same words with exactly one in-scope identifier copied exactly; instrument as locator, no speech verb, no bare "it".
3. Actor, definite descriptions and ANCHOR named outside the slot; anchor non-generic and reported verbatim; SIBLING TEST passed with the instrument wording set aside and its absolute time pin retained.
4. Time absolute; answer span QUALIFYING, not a softer ceremonial form; attribution to State or office, no agentless passive.
5. INFORMATIVENESS: no restatement, no guessable answer, no answer scaffolding, no deictic span.
6. BLOCK TEST: answer fully in the block, not from a reference, the context or metadata.
7. One smallest-unit fact; 8–20 words per rendering (max 25); figures and identifiers exact in the answer; paraphrase without drift.
8. Fewer than three passed? Output fewer. None? Output the skip.
OUTPUT (valid JSON only, no markdown): a list of up to THREE objects:
[
  {"question": "...", "question_cited": "...", "answer": "...", "question_type": "...", "anchor": "..."}
]
If no question passes every test, return exactly: [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]
- answer: the shortest span that fully and directly answers the question — for a yes/no question, the shortest span that decides it — strictly grounded in the target block.
- question_type: one of the eight values under WHAT TO ASK.
- anchor: the substantive subject anchor, a verbatim substring of the base rendering, never a generic actor.

When both are present they are the same text, not two different passages: use the version in your output language for wording and terminology, and the English version as the reference reading. [EN] Document: A/CN.9/SR.841
  Title: United Nations Commission on International Trade Law
Mr. Burman (United States of America) expressed strong support for the wording of recommendation 204. He was unwilling to engage in any further discussion of the matter.
The Chairperson said that the Working Group had discussed the question at length and that the Commission had taken a decision.
Despite the concerns expressed by some delegations, there did not seem to be majority support for reopening the debate on the substance of recommendation 204.
Moreover, she trusted that the discussion of financial contracts would allay any remaining concerns.
